t: Building a golden set: sampling, slices, size and freshness
sum: How to build the labelled eval set everything else is graded against: sampling real traffic, representative vs targeted sets, stratifying by slice and reweighting, sizing from a confidence interval (78% on 200 examples worked by hand), labelling guidelines, versioning, freshness and contamination, with SWE-bench Verified as the case.
prereq: ev1
An eval is a suite of tasks with graders; eval-driven development turns real failures into cases; regression suites should pass near 100% and capability suites measure progress.
lm14
The standard error of a pass rate p on n items is √(p(1 − p)/n), and a 95% interval is about ±1.96 standard errors; eval items must be kept out of training and prompts.
ae3
Production text can be grouped into intents or topics by clustering embeddings, and the mix of intents drifts over time.
ae5
Logged user data often contains personal information (names, emails, account numbers) that must be detected and removed or masked before reuse.
ml9
Evaluation data must be kept apart from anything used to build the model; leakage makes scores optimistic.
why:
A team evaluates its document-question-answering assistant on 150 questions an engineer wrote in an afternoon. It scores 91%. In production, users complain constantly. When someone finally reads real traffic, the questions look nothing like the eval: half are about scanned PDFs with tables, a fifth are in German, many refer to "the contract I uploaded yesterday", and a steady trickle ask things no document could answer. The 91% was accurate. It was accurate about a product nobody used.

A second team does sample from real traffic, 400 conversations at random. Their legal team asks how the assistant handles questions about contract termination, which carry real liability. There are six such cases in the set. The assistant got five right. Is that 83%? With six cases, the honest interval runs from roughly 44% to 97%. The set cannot answer the one question that matters most to the business.

A third team built an excellent set a year ago. Since then the company changed its returns policy twice, launched a new product line and opened a market in Spain. Their expected answers now mark correct replies as wrong, they have no cases for the new products, and their engineers, who have tuned the prompt against those same 300 cases for a year, can recite them.

All three teams have a golden set, a set of cases with trusted expected outputs, and all three are measuring the wrong thing with it. The golden set is the foundation of everything in this track. Graders compare against it, LLM judges are calibrated on it, and release decisions are made on scores computed from it. Its flaws propagate into every number.

This lesson covers how to build one properly. You sample real traffic, keep representative and targeted sets apart, and stratify by slice and reweight. You size the set from the confidence interval you need, worked by hand for a 78% pass rate on 200 cases. You write labelling guidelines that make "correct" unambiguous, keep the set fresh and versioned, and protect it from contamination.
primer:
A golden set is like the reference weights in a standards laboratory. Every scale in the country is calibrated against weights that are themselves calibrated against a national standard. If the reference weight is off by a gram, every scale calibrated against it is off by a gram, and no amount of careful weighing downstream fixes it. If the reference weights are all one kilogram, nobody's scale is checked at five grams or fifty kilos. A golden set plays the same role for an AI system. It must be accurate (expected answers are right), representative (it covers the inputs that actually occur, in the right proportions) and precise enough (big enough that its scores can distinguish the differences you care about).

The analogy breaks in one important place. A reference weight doesn't change, but your users do. Traffic drifts, policies change, products launch. A golden set therefore has to be maintained, more like a living test suite than a museum piece.

The pipeline from traffic to a golden set

Read it left to right. You start from real traffic, because real inputs are the only honest source. You clean it: remove duplicates (the same question pasted fifty times would dominate the set) and personal data (ae5). You group it into slices, subsets sharing a property such as intent, language or customer tier, so you can see what is there and report results per slice. You sample in two ways: at random, so the set mirrors traffic, and by stratum, so rare slices get enough cases. People label each case following written guidelines, and some cases get two labellers to check the guidelines are clear. The result is stored as a versioned set with a record of where every case came from, and part of it is held out from day-to-day use.

It helps to see how each of the three teams in the opening story broke one property. The first team's set was accurate but not representative: engineer-written questions instead of real traffic. The second team's set was representative but not precise enough where it mattered: six legal cases cannot pin down a rate. The third team's set was once all three, and then decayed: expected answers went stale, traffic moved on, and tuning against the same cases turned the set into a training set. Each step in the pipeline above exists to defend one of these properties. Sampling from traffic defends representativeness. Stratifying and sizing defend precision. Guidelines, double-labelling, versioning and refreshes defend accuracy over time.

The rest of the lesson takes each step in turn and adds the arithmetic. The central formula appeared in lm14: a pass rate p measured on n cases has a standard error of √(p(1 − p)/n). That formula decides how big the set must be overall and, more importantly, how big each slice must be.
body:
1. What goes into a case

A golden-set case has more parts than an input and an answer. A useful record looks like this:

{
  "id": "ret-0142",
  "input": {"message": "Can I return the blue jacket? Bought 2 March.",
            "context": {"order_id": "<masked>", "final_sale": false, "delivered": "2026-03-04"}},
  "expected": {"action": "answer",
               "must_include": ["return is possible", "deadline 3 April"],
               "must_not_include": ["restocking fee"]},
  "slice": {"intent": "returns", "language": "en", "tier": "standard"},
  "provenance": {"source": "prod-sample", "sampled": "2026-05-12", "method": "stratified",
                 "labelled_by": ["r07", "r12"], "guideline_version": "3.2"},
  "set_version": 7
}

Each field earns its place. The input includes all the context the system will see (account state, retrieved documents if they are fixed for the test, conversation history), because the same message with different context has a different right answer. The expected block describes correctness in a form graders can use. The slice tags allow per-slice reporting. Provenance, the record of where the case came from, lets you answer later questions: was this sampled at random or chosen because it failed? Which guideline version was it labelled under? Who labelled it?

Note that expected is not one reference reply. For open-ended outputs, a single reference text penalises correct answers that are worded differently. ev3 shows how badly word-overlap metrics behave for exactly this reason. Required facts, prohibited claims, an expected action and, where needed, a rubric are more robust.

2. Sampling real traffic

Real traffic is the best source because users do things nobody predicts. They paste whole emails, ask three questions in one message, switch languages mid-sentence, refer to things said ten turns ago, and ask questions the product was never meant to answer. Cases written by engineers are cleaner, shorter and more answerable than real ones, so they overestimate quality.

Before any traffic exists, use the closest substitute. That might be dogfooding (staff using the product), a beta, logs of the human-run process the AI will assist (support tickets answered by people), or domain experts writing questions in the voice of real users. Replace these with real traffic as soon as you have it.

Cleaning comes first. De-duplicate exact and near-exact repeats: if a broken integration sent "test" 4,000 times, random sampling would fill the set with it. (ev11 covers near-duplicate detection with MinHash; for now, normalising whitespace and case and hashing catches most repeats.) Scrub personal data: names, emails, phone numbers and account numbers are masked or replaced with realistic fakes, and the expected answers must be written against the masked version. Filter out traffic that is not in scope: health checks, internal testing, obvious spam.

Then slice. Some slice properties are metadata you already have: language, customer tier, platform, input length. Others need inference. Intent is usually found by embedding the messages and clustering them (ae3), then having a person name the clusters ("returns", "delivery status", "account access", "complaint", "out of scope"). This step is valuable on its own. The cluster sizes tell you what the product is actually used for, which is often not what the product team believed.

3. Representative sets and targeted sets

There are two legitimate reasons to include a case, and they must not be mixed.

A representative set is sampled at random from cleaned traffic. Its pass rate is an unbiased estimate of the pass rate users experience. This is the headline number: "the assistant handles 78% of conversations correctly". It is only meaningful if the sampling was random. The moment you add cases because they are interesting, the number stops estimating anything about users.

A targeted set is built on purpose to probe specific behaviour. Examples include every production failure turned into a regression case, adversarial prompts (ev9), rare but costly slices, and boundary cases experts write (a return requested on day 30 exactly). Its pass rate is a measure of how the system handles those situations. It says nothing about what fraction of users are served well, because the set is deliberately enriched with hard cases.

Here is how mixing them misleads. Suppose the representative set of 200 cases scores 78%. You add 100 failure-mined cases on which the system scores 40%. The combined score is (156 + 40)/300 = 65.3%. Next month, a change raises the representative score to 80% while the targeted score rises to 55%. The combined score is (160 + 55)/300 = 71.7%. A 6.4-point jump on the dashboard reflects mostly progress on hard cases, and only 2 points of change in what users experience. Report them as separate suites, each with its own interval.

4. Stratifying and reweighting

Random sampling has a weakness: rare slices get few cases. If a slice is 5% of traffic, a random sample of 200 contains about 10 cases from it, and an interval on 10 cases is so wide it is useless. The fix is stratified sampling: decide how many cases you want from each slice, and sample that many from within each.

Stratified sampling with equal or boosted counts per slice changes the composition of the set, so the raw pass rate no longer matches the user experience. You fix that by reweighting: compute each slice's pass rate, then combine them weighted by each slice's true share of traffic. Worked example with three slices:

SliceTraffic shareCases sampledPassedSlice pass rate
Order status70%806885.0%
Returns25%604575.0%
Legal complaints5%603355.0%
Total100%20014673.0% unweighted

The unweighted pass rate is 146/200 = 73.0%, but that over-represents the hard legal slice, which has 30% of the cases and only 5% of the traffic. The traffic-weighted estimate is 0.70 × 0.85 + 0.25 × 0.75 + 0.05 × 0.55 = 0.595 + 0.1875 + 0.0275 = 81.0%. That is the number that estimates what users experience. The 55% on legal complaints is now measured on 60 cases instead of the 10 random sampling would have given, so it is precise enough to act on.

Which slices deserve oversampling? The ones where errors are costly (legal, medical, financial, safety), the ones where the system is weak (low pass rate means more room for movement and more to learn), and the ones that matter strategically (a new market, a new enterprise customer). Slices where the system is reliably near 100% and errors are cheap can get fewer cases.

5. How precise is the set? The 78%-on-200 example

Every score computed from a golden set is an estimate. lm14 introduced the standard error of a proportion. Here is the full calculation for a pass rate of 78% on 200 representative cases, because this is the number you will be asked to defend.

The standard error (SE) is the typical amount the estimate would vary if you drew a different random 200 cases:

SE = √(p(1 − p)/n) = √(0.78 × 0.22 / 200) = √(0.1716 / 200) = √0.000858 = 0.0293, or 2.93 percentage points.

A 95% confidence interval is a range built so that, over many repetitions of the sampling, 95% of such ranges would contain the true pass rate. With the normal approximation it is p ± 1.96 × SE:

1.96 × 2.93 = 5.74 points, so the interval is 72.3% to 83.7%. The half-width, ±5.74 points, is the margin of error.

That simple interval is called the Wald interval, and it has known problems. It assumes the estimate's sampling distribution is symmetric and normal, which is roughly true for moderate p and large n and false otherwise. At 199 passes out of 200, Wald gives 99.5% ± 1.0%, an upper bound above 100%. The Wilson interval fixes this. Its formula looks heavier but is a few lines of code:

import math
def wilson(passes, n, z=1.96):
    p = passes / n
    denom = 1 + z*z/n
    centre = (p + z*z/(2*n)) / denom
    half = z * math.sqrt(p*(1-p)/n + z*z/(4*n*n)) / denom
    return centre - half, centre + half

wilson(156, 200)   # (0.7176, 0.8318)

For 156 of 200, Wilson gives 71.8% to 83.2%, slightly shifted toward 50% compared with Wald. Brown, Cai and DasGupta's 2001 study of binomial intervals showed that the Wald interval's actual coverage can fall well below its nominal 95%, erratically, even at sample sizes people consider large, and recommended Wilson-type intervals instead. Use Wilson by default for pass rates.

What does a ±5.7-point interval mean in practice? If a competitor or a new model version scores 81% on the same set, you cannot say, from the two intervals alone, that either is better. (A paired comparison on the same items is more sensitive than comparing two intervals, as lm14 showed and ev7 develops. Still, the set-level interval tells you the resolution of your instrument.)

A special case comes up constantly with safety and regression suites: zero failures. If 0 of 200 cases fail, the pass rate is 100% and the Wald interval has zero width, which is absurd. The rule of three gives an approximate 95% upper bound on the failure rate of 3/n = 3/200 = 1.5%. To claim a failure rate below 0.1% you would need about 3,000 clean cases. "We saw no failures" is a much weaker statement than it sounds.

6. Sizing the set from the precision you need

Turn the formula around. If you need a margin of error E at 95% confidence, you need

n ≈ 1.96² × p(1 − p) / E²

At p = 0.78:

Margin of error ECases needed (p = 0.78)Cases needed (worst case p = 0.5)
±5 points264385
±3 points7321,068
±2 points1,6482,401
±1 point6,5929,604

Two patterns matter. Precision costs quadratically: halving the margin quadruples the cases. And p(1 − p) is largest at 0.5, so if you don't know the pass rate in advance, plan with 0.5 and you will not be under-sized.

The bigger trap is slices. Precision is governed by the number of cases in the slice, not in the set. Split the 200 representative cases by intent:

Order status has 120 cases (98 pass, 81.7%, ±6.9 points). Returns has 50 (37 pass, 74%, ±12.2). Legal has 30 (21 pass, 70%, ±16.4). The headline looks respectable at ±5.7, but the legal slice could plausibly be anywhere from 54% to 86%. If someone asks "how good are we on legal questions?", the honest answer is "we don't know yet".

So the sizing question is really: which slices need which precision? If you need ±5 points on each of five important slices, you need around 264 cases in each, about 1,300 in total, plus the representative sample. That is a lot of labelling, which is why the cheapest precision gains come from elsewhere. Paired comparisons need far fewer cases to detect a difference between two versions than independent estimates need to pin down each one (ev7). Several trials per case remove the noise from sampling randomness, though not the noise from which cases happened to be chosen.

One more caution: the formula assumes cases are independent. If the set contains ten paraphrases of the same question, or five turns from the same conversation, those cases rise and fall together, and the effective sample size is smaller than the count. Either keep one case per underlying situation in the representative set, or compute intervals that account for the clusters (ev7 bootstraps whole clusters for this reason).

7. Labelling guidelines

The expected outputs are where the "golden" in golden set comes from, and they are only as good as the instructions labellers follow. Labelling guidelines are a document that tells a labeller, for each type of case, what a correct output is. Good guidelines contain:

  • The form of correctness for each case type. For a factual question, the exact answer and acceptable variants ("3 April", "April 3rd", "within 30 days of delivery, so by 3 April"). For an explanatory answer, the facts it must contain and claims it must not make. For a classification, the label set with definitions. For open-ended quality, a rubric with levels and an example of each.
  • The authoritative sources. Which policy document version, which knowledge base. Labellers must not answer from memory.
  • What the system should do when it can't succeed. When the question is ambiguous, out of scope or unanswerable from available information, the expected behaviour is usually to ask a clarifying question, decline, or escalate. These cases must be labelled as such, or the eval will reward confident guessing (lm15 showed how binary grading rewards guessing).
  • Worked borderline examples with the decision and the reasoning, because the borderline is where labellers diverge.

Test the guidelines before trusting the labels. Have two people independently label the same 50 items and compare. Where they disagree, either the guideline is ambiguous (fix the wording, add an example) or the case is genuinely ambiguous (either drop it or make the expected behaviour "ask for clarification"). ev5 covers how to measure this agreement properly with chance-corrected statistics. The rule of thumb from ev1 applies here too: a good case is one where two domain experts would independently reach the same verdict.

Who labels matters. Correctness in specialised domains (law, medicine, tax, a company's internal policies) needs people who know the domain. Crowd workers can judge fluency and obvious errors but will miss subtle domain mistakes, and the eval will then pass outputs that experts would fail.

8. Versioning and provenance

A golden set changes over time, so every score must say which version it was computed on. Treat the set like code. Store it in version control or a dataset registry, give each release a version number, and record in every eval report the set version alongside the system version (the release manifest from ae7).

The golden rule of comparison follows: compare system versions on the same set version. Suppose this month's report shows 85% against last month's 82%, but 30% of the set was refreshed in between. You have learned nothing about the system from those two numbers. The new cases might simply be easier. To separate the effects, run both system versions on the new set. Better still, change the set and the system in separate steps. Many teams also keep a small anchor subset that never changes, so that long-term trends remain comparable across set versions.

Provenance per case pays off when something looks wrong. If a slice's score drops, you can check whether its cases were recently added, labelled under a new guideline version, or labelled by one particular person whose labels disagree with others.

9. Keeping it fresh

Golden sets decay in three ways. Each needs its own countermeasure.

The product changes. A policy update makes expected answers wrong. The system, correctly following the new policy, now "fails" those cases. If nobody updates the set, engineers learn to ignore those failures, and then they ignore real ones too. The countermeasure is to link cases to the policy or document they depend on, so that a policy change triggers review of the dependent cases.

The traffic changes. New products, new markets and new user behaviours appear. The set no longer represents users and has no cases for what is new. The countermeasure is a scheduled refresh: every month, say, sample a fresh representative batch from recent traffic. Compare its intent mix with the set's. Add cases for new intents and retire cases for intents that have disappeared.

The team overfits to it. After months of tuning prompts against the same cases, the team has, in effect, trained on the test set. The score rises faster than real quality. The countermeasure is a held-out set: a portion, perhaps 20%, that is not used for day-to-day iteration and is consulted only for release decisions. If dev-set scores climb and held-out scores do not, you are overfitting. Rotating fresh cases into both portions slows the process.

10. Contamination

Contamination means eval items, or close variants of them, are present in data the system has seen: its training data, its prompt or its retrieval corpus. A contaminated system can recall answers instead of producing them, and the eval measures memory. lm14 and rs8 covered contamination of public benchmarks (GSM1k showed accuracy drops of up to 8% on fresh problems for some models). Here the concern is your own set, which leaks in more mundane ways:

  • Few-shot examples. Someone improving the prompt copies three eval cases, with their ideal answers, into the prompt as examples. Those three now pass trivially, and similar cases get easier.
  • Retrieval corpora. A support agent writes a help-centre article or a canned reply based on an eval case, and it gets indexed. The system retrieves the answer.
  • Fine-tuning data. The eval set, or production logs that include eval inputs, ends up in a fine-tuning dataset (ev11 covers decontaminating training data).
  • Third parties. Eval data sent to a model provider or tool vendor whose terms allow them to use it for training. Check the data-use terms of every service the eval data passes through.

Detection works by searching for overlap. Compare eval inputs and expected answers against prompts, retrieval documents and training sets, using exact n-gram overlap (shared runs of n consecutive words; the GPT-3 paper used 13-word runs for its benchmark decontamination) or embedding similarity for paraphrases. Embed a canary string in eval files. This is a unique random identifier that should never appear anywhere else, so finding it in a training corpus or a model's output proves leakage. The BIG-bench benchmark files carry such a canary. Be suspicious of any score that jumps without an obvious cause. The definitive check is to write fresh cases of the same kind and difficulty. If the system scores much lower on them than on the old ones, the old ones are compromised.

Prevention is mostly organisational. Store the set with access controls, separately from training data. Automatically de-duplicate prompts, retrieval corpora and training sets against it as part of their build pipelines. Treat any eval item found in a prompt as a bug.
deep:
Label noise biases scores, and sample size does not fix it

Suppose 5% of the golden set's expected answers are wrong. A perfect system will "fail" those 5%, so its score is capped at 95%. A system that happens to make the same mistakes as the labellers gets credit for them. Worse, label errors are rarely random. They cluster in the hardest, most ambiguous cases, which are exactly where systems differ. Increasing n shrinks the interval around a biased number. It does not move the number toward the truth. Audit labels by re-labelling a random sample with a second expert, and by reviewing every case that all system versions fail: a case nothing passes is often a labelling error.

Stratified estimates are more precise when strata differ

Stratification is not only about guaranteeing rare-slice coverage. When pass rates differ substantially between strata, a stratified estimate of the overall rate has lower variance than a simple random sample of the same size. That is because the variation between strata is removed from the error. The variance of the reweighted estimate is Σ wh² ph(1 − ph)/nh over strata h with traffic weights wh. Allocating cases in proportion to wh√(ph(1 − ph)) minimises it, a rule from survey sampling called Neyman allocation. In practice teams bend this rule toward costly slices, but knowing it lets you say why oversampling a tiny slice too hard makes the headline estimate noisier. Each case in a 5% slice gets a weight proportional to 0.05/nh, and heavily oversampled strata contribute little information to the overall rate.

Difficulty and discrimination

Not every case is equally informative. A case every system passes, or every system fails, cannot distinguish versions. Item response theory, the statistics behind standardised tests, models each item's difficulty and its discrimination (how sharply it separates strong from weak test-takers), and some benchmark builders use it to prune uninformative items. For a product golden set the practical version is simpler. Track each case's pass rate across recent system versions, and periodically review cases stuck at 0% (often label bugs or impossible tasks) or at 100% for months (fine for regression, wasted in a capability suite).

Time-based splits catch what random splits miss

If the held-out set is drawn at random from the same period as the dev set, it shares that period's topics and phrasing, so overfitting to the period goes undetected. A held-out set drawn from later traffic, a time-based split, tests whether improvements generalise to the future, which is the only thing a production system cares about. The same idea underlies contamination-resistant benchmarks that only use problems published after a model's training cutoff.

Coverage versus representativeness is a real trade-off

Product teams want coverage: a case for every feature and edge case. Statisticians want representativeness: a sample that mirrors traffic. A set built purely for coverage over-weights rare situations and misstates the user experience. A set built purely for representativeness under-tests rare, costly situations. The standard resolution is the one in this lesson: separate suites, each honest about what its number means, and reweighting when a single headline is required. Interviewers probe this because candidates who have only ever built one big mixed set cannot explain what their pass rate estimates.

Privacy and realism pull in opposite directions

The most realistic cases are verbatim user messages with their full context, and that context is often personal: names, addresses, health details, account histories. Masking can change the task. Replace a customer's name with "[NAME]" and the model may behave differently than it would with a real name, and a masked date breaks any case whose correct answer depends on that date. Good practice replaces personal values with realistic synthetic ones of the same type (a fake but plausible name, a shifted but consistent date) and writes the expected answer against the replaced version. Retention rules matter too: if your privacy policy says logs are deleted after 30 days, a golden set built from logs needs a documented legal basis to keep those cases longer, or it must be built only from scrubbed, consented or synthetic data.

The expected answer can be the wrong unit

For agents and multi-turn systems, a golden "answer" may not exist. The right unit is an end state (the booking exists with these properties) or a set of constraints on the trajectory (never refunds without confirmation). Golden sets for such systems store environment snapshots and outcome checks rather than texts. They also need careful reset logic, because a case that leaves state behind contaminates the next case.
prod:
The public case: SWE-bench Verified (OpenAI, August 2024)

SWE-bench is a benchmark built from real GitHub issues in popular Python repositories. A model is given a repository and an issue and must produce a code change; the change is graded by running unit tests that the real fix made pass. By mid-2024 it was the standard measure of coding agents, and it had exactly the golden-set problems this lesson describes. Some issue descriptions did not contain enough information to know what fix was wanted. Some tests checked details of the original fix (a specific error message, a function name) that a different, valid fix would not match. Those cases failed correct solutions, so scores understated what models could do.

OpenAI's response was a labelling operation. 93 software developers experienced in Python screened 1,699 randomly sampled cases from the test set, each case annotated independently by three developers. They followed guidelines asking whether the problem statement was well specified, whether the tests would unfairly reject valid solutions, and other issues, each rated on a severity scale from 0 to 3, with 2 and 3 counted as severe. 38.3% of cases were flagged for underspecified problem statements and 61.1% for unit tests that could unfairly reject valid solutions. In total 68.3% were filtered out. The remaining 500 cases became SWE-bench Verified. GPT-4o's best score went from 16% on the original set to 33.2% on the verified one.

Three lessons carry straight to product golden sets. First, label errors bias scores, here by half, and no amount of extra cases would have fixed that; only re-labelling did. Second, the work was done with written guidelines, a severity scale and three independent labellers per case, which is how you make labels trustworthy (ev5). Third, a verified set eventually saturates. Within about a year frontier systems were scoring above 80% on it, and harder sets were needed. Golden sets are maintained, not finished.

Failure modes in practice

The engineer-written set. Cases written by the people building the system are clean, well-formed and answerable, and they reflect what the builders think users do. Symptom: excellent offline scores and poor user feedback. Fix: sample real traffic, and compare the intent mix of the set against production clusters.

The set that silently became targeted. Every production failure was added to the main set "so we don't regress". After a year, half the set is failure-mined, and the headline pass rate is meaningless as an estimate of user experience. Fix: split the suites retroactively using provenance. If there is no provenance, start recording it now.

Stale expected answers. After a policy change, 12% of cases expect the old behaviour. The team "fixes" the regressions by reverting the system to the old policy, or learns to ignore red cases. Fix: link cases to the documents they depend on, and review them when those documents change.

Personal data in the eval set. Logged conversations copied into the set with names, emails and order numbers intact, then shared with vendors and contractors. Fix: scrub at ingestion, and audit the set periodically with a personal-data detector (ae5).

What to track about the set itself

A golden set is an asset, and its health is worth a dashboard section of its own. Track the number of cases per slice and the interval width that gives; the age distribution of cases and the date of the last refresh; the intent mix of the set against the last 30 days of traffic; the share of cases that every recent system version fails (probable label bugs); the double-labelled sample's agreement rate; and the dev-versus-held-out gap.
myths: The golden set should be as big as possible.

Its size should come from the precision you need, and its quality matters more than its count. With 200 cases at around 78% the 95% interval is about ±5.7 points; to halve that you need four times as many cases. Thousands of carelessly labelled cases give a precise estimate of the wrong thing, because label errors bias the score and no sample size fixes bias.
Sampling production at random gives you a good eval set.

It gives you a representative set, which is exactly right for estimating the overall pass rate, and nearly useless for rare but important slices: if legal complaints are 2% of traffic, 200 random cases contain about 4 of them. You need a random set for the headline number and deliberate oversampling of important slices, with reweighting when you combine them.
Once the expected answers are written, the golden set is done.

Products change (new policies, new features), so expected answers go stale; traffic changes, so the set stops representing users; and teams tune against the set, so it overfits. A golden set is a maintained asset with versions, an owner, a refresh schedule and a held-out portion.
Hard cases you found from complaints should be mixed into the main set.

Mix them in and your headline pass rate no longer estimates what users experience, because the set is now enriched with failures. Keep failure-mined and adversarial cases in separate, clearly named suites, and keep the representative set representative.
Contamination is only a problem for public benchmarks.

Private sets leak too: an eval example gets pasted into the prompt as a few-shot example, a support macro containing the answer is added to the retrieval index, or the eval set is used as fine-tuning data. Any of these turns the eval into a memory test. Leaks are usually found only when a score jumps for no reason.

recap: A golden set is a carefully labelled set of cases whose expected outputs or verdicts you trust; it is what graders compare against and what cheaper graders are calibrated on.
Build it from real traffic (or the closest thing), de-duplicated and scrubbed of personal data, with expected behaviour written by people who know the domain.
Keep two kinds of set apart: a representative set sampled at random to estimate the overall pass rate, and targeted sets (failure-mined, adversarial, rare slices) to probe specific behaviour.
Stratify by slice and oversample important rare slices, then reweight by real traffic shares when combining; in the worked example the unweighted 73% becomes a traffic-weighted 81%.
A 78% pass rate on 200 cases has a standard error of 2.9 points and a 95% interval of about 72% to 84% (Wilson: 71.8% to 83.2%); a ±2-point interval needs about 1,650 cases.
Precision per slice depends on the slice's own size, so a 30-case slice at 70% has an interval of about ±16 points: decide which slices need which precision and size them accordingly.
Labelling guidelines say what correct means for each case type (exact answer, required facts, acceptable alternatives, rubric) and are tested by having two labellers label the same items.

Version the set, record its provenance, refresh it from recent traffic on a schedule, keep a held-out portion for release decisions, and guard it against leaking into prompts, retrieval, and training data.
glossary: Canary string
A unique random string embedded in eval files so that their presence in training data or model outputs can be searched for later.
Confidence interval
A range computed from a sample that, by construction, contains the true value in a stated share (e.g. 95%) of repeated samples.
Contamination
Eval items or close variants appearing in data the system was trained, prompted or retrieved on, so it can recall answers instead of producing them.
Golden set
A carefully labelled eval set whose expected outputs or verdicts are trusted as the reference.
Held-out set
A portion of the golden set not used for day-to-day tuning, consulted only for major decisions, to detect overfitting to the main set.
Labelling guidelines
The written instructions that tell labellers what a correct output is for each type of case, with examples and edge cases.
Margin of error
Half the width of a confidence interval: ±E around the estimate.
Provenance
The record of where each case came from (source, date, sampling method, who labelled it).
Representative set
A set sampled at random from real traffic, so its pass rate estimates the pass rate users experience.
Rule of three
If 0 failures are seen in n independent trials, an approximate 95% upper bound on the failure rate is 3/n.
Slice
A subset of cases sharing a property (intent, language, customer tier, input length) whose results are reported separately.
Standard error
The standard deviation of an estimate across repeated samples; for a proportion, √(p(1 − p)/n).
Stratified sampling
Dividing traffic into slices and sampling a chosen number from each, rather than sampling the whole population at random.
Targeted set
A set built deliberately to probe specific behaviour: past failures, adversarial inputs, rare slices. Its pass rate does not estimate the user experience.
Wald interval
The simple interval p ± z·√(p(1 − p)/n); inaccurate for small n or for p near 0 or 1.
Wilson interval
A confidence interval for a proportion that stays inside 0-1 and behaves well for small samples and extreme rates.
drill:
Design: a golden set for a contract-review assistant

A legal-tech company's assistant answers questions about uploaded contracts ("What's the termination notice period?", "Is there an auto-renewal clause?"). It handles about 8,000 questions a week. 60% are about dates and notice periods, 25% about obligations and liability, 10% are summaries, and 5% are questions the contract can't answer. Lawyers' time costs $150 an hour and they can label about 20 cases an hour. The head of legal wants to know, with a margin of ±5 points, how accurate the assistant is on liability questions specifically, and the CEO wants a single headline number. You have a budget of $15,000 for labelling. Design the set.

Answer

Budget to cases. $15,000 / $150 = 100 lawyer-hours × 20 = 2,000 labels. Reserve about 20% for double-labelling (checking guidelines and measuring agreement) and for refreshes, which leaves about 1,600 single-labelled cases to build the set.

Liability slice precision. If the pass rate is unknown, plan at p = 0.5: n = 1.96² × 0.25 / 0.05² ≈ 385. If a pilot suggests around 80%, n ≈ 246. Allocate about 300 liability cases. That gives ±5 points even at a pass rate somewhat below 80%.

Representative set for the headline. Draw about 400 questions at random from production, de-duplicated and with client names masked. This gives ±4-5 points on the headline and naturally includes about 20 unanswerable questions.

Other strata. Fill the rest (about 900) with stratified samples. About 300 for dates and notice periods (high volume, and errors here are costly). About 200 summaries, graded with a rubric of required clauses and prohibited invented ones. About 150 unanswerable questions, where the expected behaviour is "the contract does not say", to measure false confident answers (lm15). And a targeted suite of about 250 for known failures, such as scanned PDFs with tables and amended contracts. Keep that suite separate from the headline.

Headline. Compute it from the random 400 alone, or combine all strata reweighted by the 60/25/10/5 traffic shares. Report it with a Wilson interval. Report every slice with its own interval.

Guidelines and quality. Expected answers are written as the exact value plus the clause reference, and lawyers must cite the clause. Have two lawyers double-label 150 cases. Disagreements go to adjudication, and the guidelines are revised before full labelling begins.

Maintenance. Hold out 20%. Version the set. Refresh 10% quarterly from new traffic. Keep contracts used in the set out of any fine-tuning data and out of the few-shot examples.
qa: E
What is a golden set and what is it for?

A golden set is a labelled set of cases whose expected outputs or verdicts you trust. It has two jobs: it is the reference graders compare against when you evaluate a system version, and it is the ground truth you calibrate cheaper graders, like LLM judges, on. Everything downstream inherits its quality, so labelling errors in it become errors in every decision.
E
Where should eval cases come from?

From real traffic wherever possible: production logs, a beta, or dogfooding, because real users send messier, more varied inputs than anyone imagines. De-duplicate, remove personal data, and cluster by intent to see what is there. Then add targeted cases: every production failure, edge cases domain experts know about, and adversarial inputs. Synthetic generation fills gaps but should not be the core, because generated inputs are cleaner and more uniform than real ones.
E
Compute a 95% confidence interval for a 78% pass rate on 200 cases.

The standard error is √(0.78 × 0.22 / 200) = √0.000858 ≈ 0.0293, or 2.9 points. 1.96 × 2.93 ≈ 5.7, so the interval is about 72.3% to 83.7%. The Wilson interval, which behaves better for small samples, gives 71.8% to 83.2%. Either way, a competitor scoring 81% on the same set is not distinguishable from you on this evidence alone.
M
How many cases do you need?

Work backwards from the precision the decision needs. For a margin of error E at 95% confidence, n ≈ 1.96² × p(1 − p) / E². At p = 0.78: ±5 points needs about 264 cases, ±3 about 732, ±2 about 1,650, ±1 about 6,600. Use p = 0.5 if you have no idea, which is the worst case. And this is per slice: if you need ±5 points on each of five slices, you need about 264 in each, not 264 overall.

Follow-up: That's a lot of labelling. How else can you get precision? — Paired comparisons on the same items need far fewer cases to detect a difference between versions than independent estimates do (ev7), and several trials per case remove sampling noise, though not case-selection noise.
M
What is the difference between a representative set and a targeted set, and why keep them apart?

A representative set is sampled at random from traffic, so its pass rate estimates what users experience. A targeted set is built on purpose (past failures, adversarial prompts, rare slices) to probe behaviour; its pass rate means nothing about users because it's enriched with hard cases. Mixing them makes the headline number uninterpretable: adding 100 failure-mined cases to 200 random ones drags the score down and hides whether real quality moved. Report them as separate suites.
Follow-up: Can you combine them into one number? — Only by reweighting each stratum by its true traffic share; otherwise report them separately.
M
A slice that matters (legal complaints) is 2% of traffic. How do you evaluate it?

Random sampling would give about 4 such cases in 200, an interval of ±40 points, so it's useless. Stratify: sample a fixed number from the slice, say 60, found by an intent classifier or keyword filter plus human confirmation. Report the slice's pass rate with its own interval. When computing the overall rate, weight the slice by its 2% traffic share so oversampling doesn't distort the headline.

Follow-up: What if the slice is so rare you can't find 60 real examples? — Ask domain experts to write realistic ones, generate variants of the few real ones and have experts review them, and label them clearly as constructed so their pass rate isn't mistaken for a production estimate.
M
What goes into labelling guidelines for a golden set?

For each case type, what correct means: an exact expected answer, a set of acceptable answers, a list of facts the answer must contain and claims it must not make, or a rubric with levels and examples. Plus how to handle ambiguous inputs (what should the system do when the question can't be answered?), which sources are authoritative, and worked examples of borderline cases with the decision and its reason. Test the guidelines by having two people label the same 50 items; disagreements show where they're ambiguous.

Follow-up: How do you store expected outputs for open-ended answers? — As required facts and prohibited claims, or a rubric, not a single reference text, because a single reference penalises correct answers worded differently.
M
How do you keep a golden set fresh?

Version it and record provenance per case. On a schedule (monthly, say), sample recent production into it, stratified by intent, so new intents and products appear. Review expected answers when the product or policy changes, because stale answers grade correct behaviour as wrong. Retire cases that no longer reflect anything users do. Keep a held-out portion that isn't used for day-to-day tuning, and compare dev and held-out scores to detect overfitting.

Follow-up: If you change the set, how do you compare this month's score to last month's? — Re-run the old system version on the new set; compare versions on the same set version, never across set versions.
H
How can a private golden set become contaminated, and how do you detect it?

Through few-shot examples copied from it into the prompt, retrieval indexes that ingest documents containing the answers (a support macro written from an eval case), fine-tuning on data that includes eval items or their paraphrases, or sending eval data to a provider whose terms allow training on it. Detection: n-gram or embedding overlap between eval items and prompts, retrieval corpora and training data; canary strings embedded in eval files; and suspicion of sudden jumps. A check that works well is to write fresh cases of the same kind; if the system scores much worse on them, the old ones are compromised.

Follow-up: How would you prevent it organisationally? — Store the set with access controls, separate from training data pipelines, automatically de-duplicate prompts, indexes and training sets against it, and treat any eval item showing up in a prompt as a bug.
H
Your overall pass rate went from 82% to 85% after a change, but you refreshed 30% of the set the same week. What can you conclude?

Nothing about the change from those two numbers, because both the system and the measuring stick changed. Run the old and new system on the same, new set version, ideally with paired analysis, and separately run the new system on the old set version. If the old system also scores higher on the new set, the refresh made the set easier. Then the 3 points belong to the set, not the change.

Follow-up: How do you prevent this confusion? — Freeze the set version in every eval report, change set and system in separate steps, and keep a long-lived anchor subset that never changes so trends over months remain comparable.
H
Why might an interval computed as p ± 1.96·SE be wrong, and what do you use instead?

That Wald interval assumes the sampling distribution is roughly normal, which fails when n is small or p is near 0 or 1: at 199 of 200 passing it gives an upper bound above 100% and a lower bound that is too optimistic. The Wilson interval fixes this and should be the default for pass rates. Also, the formula assumes cases are independent; if cases come in clusters (ten variants of one template, multiple turns of one conversation), the effective sample size is smaller and the interval must be widened, for example with a clustered standard error or by bootstrapping clusters. With zero failures in n, the rule of three gives an approximate 95% upper bound of 3/n.
Follow-up: 0 failures in 200 safety cases. What do you report? — That the failure rate is likely below 3/200 = 1.5%, not that it's zero; showing it's below 0.1% needs about 3,000 clean cases.
H
Design the golden set for a new multilingual support assistant expected to handle 20,000 conversations a week in 6 languages.

Start with whatever real data exists (beta, existing human-agent chats), cluster by intent and language, and draw a representative set of about 300 conversations at random for the headline rate. Then stratify: for each language-and-top-intent cell that matters, ensure at least 40-60 cases, oversampling minority languages, and reweight by traffic share when combining. Add a targeted suite of past failures, escalation-worthy cases and adversarial prompts. Have native-speaker domain experts write expected behaviour as required facts and prohibited claims, with guidelines tested on a 50-item double-labelled sample per language. Version it, refresh 10-20% monthly from production, keep 20% held out, and de-duplicate prompts and retrieval data against it.

Follow-up: Budget allows only 1,200 labelled cases in total. Where do you spend them? — Weight toward slices where errors are costly and where the system is weakest, since slices sitting at 98% need fewer cases to confirm; and use the judge (validated on a subset) to grade the rest of the traffic.
refs: 93 developers screened 1,699 samples, each by three annotators; 68.3% were filtered out; the 500-case result doubled GPT-4o's score versus the original set.
SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues? (Jimenez et al., 2023)
The original benchmark built from real repository issues and their tests; the source the Verified subset was curated from.
Interval Estimation for a Binomial Proportion (Brown, Cai & DasGupta, 2001)
Why the textbook Wald interval misbehaves and why Wilson-type intervals are preferred.
Beyond the Imitation Game (BIG-bench, Srivastava et al., 2022)
A large benchmark that embeds a canary string in its files so training corpora can be checked for contamination.
Demystifying evals for AI agents (Anthropic Engineering, 2026)
Practical guidance on sourcing tasks from real failures, balanced sets, and tasks two experts would grade the same way.

t: Metrics for generative output: from exact match to pass@k
sum: Which number to compute for which kind of output: normalised exact match and token F1, field-level scores for structured output, BLEU and ROUGE worked by hand and why they fail, embedding similarity and BERTScore, task-specific checks such as execution, the unbiased pass@k estimator, and calibrated scores, with the Codex/HumanEval paper as the case.
prereq: ev1

An eval runs tasks through the system and scores each output with graders; assertions are the cheapest graders and should be used wherever a requirement is crisp; pass@k counts at least one success in k trials.
ev2
A golden set stores expected behaviour as exact answers, required facts, prohibited claims or rubrics; a single reference text penalises correct answers worded differently.
ml7
Precision is the share of flagged items that are right, recall the share of right items that are flagged, and F1 their harmonic mean.
ml15
A calibrated score means what it says: among items given 0.8, about 80% are positive; reliability diagrams and expected calibration error measure it.
lm10
An embedding maps text to a vector so that similar meanings are close; cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors.
why:
A team building a meeting-summary feature needs a number to track. They pick ROUGE, the standard summarisation metric, which measures how many words of a reference summary appear in the generated one. They write reference summaries for 300 meetings and start iterating. Over two months ROUGE climbs from 0.38 to 0.46, and they ship the latest model with a celebratory post. Within a week, users complain that summaries attribute decisions to the wrong people and include action items nobody agreed to. When someone reads the outputs, the pattern is obvious. The new model learned to write in the exact style of the reference summaries ("The team agreed that... Action item: ... will ...") and to fill that template with plausible details. ROUGE rewarded the style. It could not see the errors.

A second team built a coding assistant and measured it by comparing generated code to reference solutions with BLEU, a word-overlap metric from machine translation. The code that scored highest was code that looked like the reference, and a fair amount of it didn't run. When OpenAI introduced its Codex code models in 2021, the paper made this explicit: functionally wrong programs often had higher BLEU scores than correct ones. That is why they evaluated by running unit tests instead.

Both teams made the same mistake. They chose a metric because it was standard and easy to compute, not because it measured what made an output good. Every eval needs a number. Choosing which number to compute, for which kind of output, and knowing exactly how it can lie, is the subject of this lesson.

It goes from the most closed outputs to the most open. It starts with exact match and the normalisation that makes it work, then token F1 for partial credit, and field-level scores for structured output. Then BLEU and ROUGE, computed by hand so their failures are visible, and embedding similarity and BERTScore. Then task-specific checks such as execution, which are the best automated metrics when they exist, and the pass@k estimator for sampled outputs. Last, calibration: what it means for a score to mean what it says. Judgement-based grading by LLMs gets its own topic next (ev4).
primer:
Think of choosing a metric like choosing how to mark an exam. A multiple-choice question is marked by comparing the letter to the key: fast, objective, no judgement needed. A short-answer question ("name the capital of Australia") is marked against a list of acceptable answers, with some tolerance for spelling. A maths problem might get partial credit for method. An essay needs a marker with a rubric. Nobody would mark an essay by counting how many words it shares with a model essay. Yet that is what BLEU and ROUGE do when applied to open-ended LLM output.

The analogy breaks in one place, and it helps. With an exam, the question type is given. With an LLM feature, you design the output, and you can often turn an essay question into several short-answer ones. If the support assistant returns a JSON object with an action field and a refund_days field, and a prose reply, then the action and the number can be marked like multiple choice. Only the prose needs a rubric. Designing outputs so that more of them can be checked mechanically is the single most effective thing you can do for evaluation.

The spectrum of metrics

On the closed end, the output is a label, a number, an entity or an action, and exact match after normalisation is ideal. A little further along are text spans, such as an extracted quote or a name with a title, where token F1 gives partial credit. Structured outputs are graded field by field. Executable outputs, code and SQL, are graded by running them, which is the gold standard of automated evaluation because it checks behaviour rather than form. Then come translations and summaries, where the traditional metrics, BLEU and ROUGE, compare words against a reference, and embedding-based metrics compare meanings. These are cheap but weak, for reasons we will compute. On the open end, chat replies and explanations need a rubric applied by a human or an LLM judge.

Before trusting any metric, ask it three questions. What does it reward? ROUGE rewards sharing words with the reference, which is not the same as being right. How can an output score well while being bad, or badly while being good? Every metric in this lesson has a concrete answer, and the body works one example for each. Has anyone checked it against human judgement on this task? A metric validated for news translation in 2002 has not been validated for your insurance chatbot. Metrics that survive all three questions for your outputs are the ones to gate on. The others are diagnostics at best.

Two ideas recur throughout. First, a metric is a model of what good means, and every metric has a characteristic way of being fooled. Know it before you trust the number. Second, the number has to support a decision. A metric that moves when quality moves, and stays still when it doesn't, is valid. One that moves with style, length or wording is measuring something else.
body:
1. Exact match and the normalisation that makes it work

Exact match (EM) scores 1 if the prediction equals an acceptable answer and 0 otherwise. Stated that baldly, it sounds uselessly strict: "Canberra." with a full stop would fail against "Canberra". So EM is always computed after normalisation, transforming both sides to a canonical form. The conventions popularised by the SQuAD reading-comprehension benchmark are a good base: lower-case everything, remove punctuation, remove the articles "a", "an" and "the", and collapse whitespace. For LLM features you usually add domain rules: numbers to a standard format ("1,000", "1000" and "one thousand" all become 1000), dates to ISO format (2026-04-03), units converted, known aliases mapped ("USA", "United States", "U.S." become one value).

import re, string
def normalise(s: str) -> str:
    s = s.lower()
    s = "".join(ch for ch in s if ch not in string.punctuation)
    s = re.sub(r"\b(a|an|the)\b", " ", s)
    return " ".join(s.split())

def exact_match(pred: str, golds: list[str]) -> int:
    return int(any(normalise(pred) == normalise(g) for g in golds))

Notice golds is a list. Many questions have several acceptable answers, and the golden set (ev2) should record them all.

With LLMs there is a step before normalisation: answer extraction. Models rarely reply with just the answer. They say "Based on the policy, you have 30 days, so the deadline is 3 April." To compare with the gold "3 April", you have to find the answer in the text. The options, from most to least robust, are these. You can ask for structured output with an answer field. You can ask the model to end with a fixed marker ("Final answer: ...") and parse after it. Or you can write a regex for the expected type, such as the last date in the text. Each fallback adds a way for a correct answer to score 0. Extraction failures look exactly like model errors in the aggregate. Teams have spent weeks "improving the model" when the real problem was that a new model version wrote "Final Answer:" with a capital A. The defence is to log extraction failures separately and to read a sample of zeros before acting on them.

2. Token F1: partial credit for spans

Sometimes a prediction is partly right. The gold answer is "Eiffel Tower" and the model says "the Eiffel Tower in Paris". EM gives 0, which is harsh. Token F1 treats the prediction and gold as bags of tokens and computes precision and recall over them (ml7), after normalisation.

Worked: normalised, the prediction is [eiffel, tower, in, paris] (the article is removed) and the gold is [eiffel, tower]. The overlap is 2 tokens.

  • Precision = overlap / prediction tokens = 2/4 = 0.50. Half of what the model said is in the gold.
  • Recall = overlap / gold tokens = 2/2 = 1.00. All of the gold is in what the model said.
  • F1 = 2PR/(P + R) = 2 × 0.5 × 1.0 / 1.5 = 0.67.

With multiple gold answers, take the maximum F1 over them. Token F1 is well suited to extractive tasks, where the answer is a span of a document. It is poorly suited to anything where word order or a single word changes the meaning. "Not eligible" and "eligible" have F1 0.67, and "5 to 7 days" and "7 to 5 days" have F1 1.0.

Long, chatty LLM answers also distort F1. A correct answer buried in a three-sentence explanation has terrible precision. So for LLM outputs, extract the answer first and compute F1 on the extracted span, or ask for a short answer field.

3. Structured output: schema validity and field-level scores

When the output is structured, such as JSON from an extraction model, evaluation splits into two layers that should be reported separately.

Schema validity asks whether the output parses and conforms to the schema: required fields present, types right, enums in range. This is a pass/fail assertion and its rate is a metric in itself. A model that produces invalid JSON 3% of the time has a 3% hard-failure rate in production, whatever its field accuracy.

Field-level scores compare each field with its gold value, after field-appropriate normalisation: dates to ISO, amounts to decimals with two places, names trimmed and case-folded. Worked, for one invoice:

FieldGoldPredictedOutcome
invoice_numberINV-2291INV-2291correct (TP)
date2026-03-0404/03/2026 → 2026-03-04correct after normalising (TP)
total1,240.001240.0correct (TP)
vendorAcme LtdAcme Limitedwrong unless aliases map it (FP + FN)
po_number(absent)PO-778invented (FP)
tax206.67(missing)missed (FN)

Counting a correct field as a true positive (TP), a predicted value that is wrong or invented as a false positive (FP), and a gold value not correctly predicted as a false negative (FN): TP = 3, FP = 2 (vendor, po_number), FN = 2 (vendor, tax). Precision = 3/5 = 0.60, recall = 3/5 = 0.60, F1 = 0.60. Over many invoices you sum the counts (micro-average) or average per field (macro-average). The macro view matters more, because the average hides per-field problems. A system can score 0.95 overall while getting the total amount right only 80% of the time, and the total is the field that costs money.

The invented PO number deserves its own counter. Hallucinated fields (lm15) are usually worse than missing ones, because downstream systems trust them.

4. BLEU, computed by hand

BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy, Papineni et al., 2002) was designed to rank machine-translation systems cheaply. It compares a candidate translation with one or more reference translations by counting shared n-grams, runs of n consecutive words.

The recipe, for n = 1 to 4: count the candidate's n-grams that appear in the reference, clipping each n-gram's count at the number of times it appears in the reference (so "the the the the" can't score by repeating a common word). Divide by the candidate's total number of n-grams. That gives four modified precisions, p1 to p4. BLEU is their geometric mean multiplied by a brevity penalty (BP), which punishes candidates shorter than the reference: BP = 1 if the candidate is longer than the reference, otherwise exp(1 − r/c), with r the reference length and c the candidate length.

BLEU = BP × exp((ln p1 + ln p2 + ln p3 + ln p4)/4)

Worked, reference "the cat is on the mat", candidate "the cat sat on the mat":

nCandidate n-gramsMatches (clipped)pn
1the, cat, sat, on, the, matthe ×2, cat, on, mat = 55/6
2the cat, cat sat, sat on, on the, the matthe cat, on the, the mat = 33/5
3the cat sat, cat sat on, sat on the, on the maton the mat = 11/4
4the cat sat on, cat sat on the, sat on the matnone0/3

Both sentences have 6 words, so BP = 1. But p4 = 0 and ln 0 is minus infinity, so BLEU = 0 for a sentence that differs from the reference by one word. That is why BLEU was defined at the corpus level, pooling n-gram counts across a whole test set before dividing, and why sentence-level BLEU needs smoothing. With a simple add-one smoothing on each precision, the candidate scores about 0.49.

Now the failure. Score two more candidates against the same reference, with the same smoothing:

  • "a cat was sitting on the rug", a reasonable paraphrase, though "rug" isn't quite "mat": about 0.26.
  • "the cat is not on the mat", the opposite meaning: about 0.50.

The candidate that contradicts the reference scores highest, because it contains the reference word for word plus one extra word. BLEU measures surface similarity to one particular wording. It knows nothing about meaning.

5. ROUGE, and the refund example

ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation, Lin, 2004) was designed for summarisation and is recall-oriented: what fraction of the reference's content does the candidate cover? ROUGE-N is n-gram recall: matching n-grams divided by the reference's n-grams. ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence (LCS), the longest sequence of words that appears in both texts in the same order, not necessarily adjacent. From it, precision = LCS/candidate length, recall = LCS/reference length, and an F-score combines them.

Here is a case that matters for a support assistant. The reference answer is "refunds are processed within 5 to 7 business days" (9 words). Three candidates:

CandidateCorrect?LCSROUGE-L FROUGE-1 recall
"refunds are processed within 2 to 3 business days"No: wrong number70.787/9
"your refund will arrive in 5 to 7 business days"Yes50.535/9
"it takes about a week for the money to reach your account"Yes, roughly10.101/9

Check the first row by hand. The longest common subsequence is "refunds are processed within to business days", 7 words, so precision is 7/9, recall is 7/9 and F = 0.78. The wrong answer wins by a wide margin. The one word that makes it wrong is the one word ROUGE doesn't care about. The colloquial correct answer scores almost nothing.

6. Why overlap metrics fail for LLM output, and where they still help

The examples show four failure mechanisms.

Paraphrase. A correct answer in different words scores low. Modern LLMs paraphrase freely, so the variance of BLEU and ROUGE across correct answers is huge.

Meaning-critical tokens are cheap. A negation, a number or a name is one token among many, so getting it wrong costs little overlap.

One reference is not the answer space. The metrics compare with the references you wrote. If there are many good answers, as there almost always are for open-ended output, every good answer that isn't close to a reference is punished.

They can be gamed by style. Optimising against ROUGE teaches a model the references' style, as the meeting-summary team discovered.

The Codex paper showed the code version of this: programs that were functionally wrong (they disagreed with the reference solution on some input) often had higher BLEU than functionally correct ones. Code makes the point vivid because correctness can be checked objectively. The same thing happens, less visibly, in prose.

Overlap metrics still have uses. They are cheap regression detectors when the output is meant to stay close to a fixed text. Examples are templated messages, translations of short UI strings, and a model that should reproduce a clause verbatim. A sudden change in average ROUGE between two versions says that something changed, worth a look. And for machine translation at corpus level, with several references, metrics in the BLEU family remain a standard sanity check. They should not be the decision metric for an LLM feature's quality.

7. Embedding similarity and BERTScore

The obvious fix for paraphrase is to compare meanings rather than words. An embedding model (lm10) maps a text to a vector such that texts with similar meanings land close together. Cosine similarity measures closeness: the dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their lengths. It is 1 for identical directions and around 0 for unrelated ones. Worked with toy 3-dimensional vectors a = (0.8, 0.5, 0.1) and b = (0.7, 0.6, 0.2): the dot product is 0.56 + 0.30 + 0.02 = 0.88; |a| = √0.90 = 0.949 and |b| = √0.89 = 0.943; cosine = 0.88 / (0.949 × 0.943) = 0.983. Real embeddings have hundreds or thousands of dimensions, but the arithmetic is the same.

Comparing the embedding of an answer with the embedding of the reference does credit paraphrases. "Your refund will arrive in 5 to 7 business days" and "refunds are processed within 5 to 7 business days" will be very close. But the wrong answer, "within 2 to 3 business days", is also very close, because it shares the topic, the structure and almost all the meaning. So does "refunds are not processed within 5 to 7 days". Embeddings capture what a text is about far better than whether it is right. That makes them excellent for retrieval and clustering, and weak as correctness metrics.

BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2019) refines the idea at the token level. Each token in the candidate and reference gets a contextual embedding from a BERT-style model. Each candidate token is matched to its most similar reference token (greedy matching by cosine). Averaging those best-match similarities gives precision; the same from the reference side gives recall; and F1 combines them. Optional idf weighting gives rare, content-bearing words more say. The authors also rescale scores against a baseline, because raw values bunch in a narrow high range. BERTScore correlates better with human judgements than BLEU on several benchmarks, because it credits synonyms and paraphrases. It shares the embedding blind spot: a single flipped number or added "not" barely changes the token matches.

If you use similarity metrics, two rules apply. First, raw values have no meaning on their own. A cosine of 0.83 might be "same answer" for one embedding model and "loosely related" for another. Calibrate a threshold by labelling a few hundred pairs as equivalent or not and choosing the threshold that best separates them, then report the precision and recall of the metric as a classifier. Second, pair them with checks for the things they miss: an exact-match check on extracted numbers and entities, or a negation-aware judge.

8. Task-specific checks: the best automated metrics

Whenever an output can be checked by doing something with it, that check beats any comparison with a reference. The principle is functional correctness: judge the output by whether it works.

  • Code: run it against unit tests in a sandbox. HumanEval, introduced in the Codex paper, has 164 hand-written problems with an average of 7.7 tests each. Hand-written, because the models were trained on so much public code that problems copied from the internet might already be memorised.
  • SQL: execute the generated query and the reference query on the same database and compare result sets (order-insensitive unless the question asks for an order). Use several database states, because a wrong query can return the right rows on a small test database by accident.
  • Maths and numeric answers: extract the final number and compare within a tolerance, or check symbolic equivalence.
  • Tool and API calls: check the function name and arguments against the expected call, with normalisation for argument order and formats, or execute against a mock and check the resulting state.
  • Citations: check that every cited document ID exists and was retrieved, and, with a judge or entailment model, that the cited passage supports the claim (ev6).
  • Format and constraints: length limits, required sections, allowed vocabulary, language detection, banned content patterns.

Task-specific checks have their own failure: weak tests. If a function has two thin unit tests, wrong code passes by accident. If tests encode one particular implementation (an exact error message), valid alternatives fail, which is what SWE-bench Verified found in 61% of the cases it screened (ev2). Test the tests: deliberately break the reference solution in small ways (mutation testing) and check the tests catch it, and review cases where every system fails.

9. pass@k: sampled outputs and the unbiased estimator

ev1 defined pass@k as the probability that at least one of k samples succeeds. For a single task with known per-sample success probability p, it is 1 − (1 − p)k. In practice you don't know p for each problem. You estimate it by drawing samples, and the obvious estimation shortcut is biased.

The Codex paper's estimator: for each problem, generate n ≥ k samples (they used n = 200 for k up to 100), count the number c that pass the tests, and compute

pass@k = 1 − C(n − c, k) / C(n, k)

where C(a, b) is the number of ways to choose b items from a. The fraction is the probability that a random subset of k of your n samples contains no correct sample. Subtracting from one gives the probability that it contains at least one. Average this over problems.

Worked, n = 10 samples, c = 3 correct:

  • k = 1: 1 − C(7,1)/C(10,1) = 1 − 7/10 = 0.30. For k = 1 it reduces to c/n, as it should.
  • k = 5: C(7,5) = 21 and C(10,5) = 252, so 1 − 21/252 = 1 − 0.083 = 0.917.
  • The plug-in formula 1 − (1 − 0.3)5 = 0.832 gives a different answer. The paper shows in an appendix that this plug-in is biased.

The bigger bias comes from computing pass@k from an average pass@1 across problems. Take two problems, one the model always solves (p = 1.0) and one it never solves (p = 0.0). Average pass@1 is 0.5. Plugging 0.5 into 1 − (1 − p)5 gives 0.97. But the true pass@5 is still 0.5: five tries at the impossible problem still fail. Problems differ in difficulty, so pass@k must be computed per problem and then averaged. This is an instance of Jensen's inequality, which says the average of a curved function is not the function of the average.

For a sense of scale, the Codex paper reports that its 12-billion-parameter Codex model solved 28.8% of HumanEval problems with one sample, and 70.2% when 100 samples were drawn per problem and a problem counted as solved if any passed. The paper's own framing is that pass@k with large k is meaningful only if something can pick the right sample. When they instead picked the sample with the highest mean log-probability, which needs no tests, results fell well short of the oracle. That is the pass@k against pass^k distinction from ev1 again. Report the k that matches how the product chooses among samples.

10. Calibrated scores

Many graders and systems produce a score rather than a verdict: a classifier's probability, a judge's 1-10 rating, a model's stated confidence. A score is calibrated if it means what it says: among outputs scored 0.8, about 80% are correct (ml15). Calibration matters for evaluation in two places. Scores used as thresholds ("send outputs with confidence below 0.7 to a human") only work if the threshold means what you think. And estimates computed from scores ("average judge probability of correctness is 0.85, so we're 85% correct") are only right if the scores are calibrated.

Checking calibration means binning items by score and comparing each bin's average score with its observed accuracy. Worked, 200 answers from a system that states its confidence, checked against gold labels:

Confidence binItemsAverage confidenceActually correctAccuracyGap
High1200.92960.800.12
Medium500.75360.720.03
Low300.55180.600.05

The expected calibration error (ECE) weights each bin's gap by its share of items: (120 × 0.12 + 50 × 0.03 + 30 × 0.05)/200 = (14.4 + 1.5 + 1.5)/200 = 17.4/200 = 0.087, about 9 points. Most of it comes from the high bin, where the system says 92% and delivers 80%: classic overconfidence. Plotting accuracy against confidence per bin gives a reliability diagram, and a calibrated system's points lie on the diagonal.

What do you do with a miscalibrated score? If the ranking is good (higher scores really are more often correct) but the values are off, fit a monotone mapping from score to observed accuracy on held-out labelled data. Platt scaling and isotonic regression (ml15) are the usual tools, and temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017) is the one-parameter version for model probabilities. Then re-check on fresh data. If you use scores for selective answering (answer only when confident, otherwise abstain or escalate), report the trade-off as coverage against accuracy. In the table, answering only the medium and high bins covers 170/200 = 85% of questions at (96 + 36)/170 = 77.6% accuracy, against 75% when answering everything. That is a small gain, because the high bin is overconfident. Calibrating it first would let you pick a better threshold.

A judge's 1-10 score is not a probability at all. It is an ordinal label, and different judges and prompts use the scale differently. If you need "probability a human would accept this", fit that mapping from judge scores to human verdicts on labelled data, exactly as above. ev4 discusses why binary judge questions are often better than scales in the first place.

11. Choosing the metric: a summary

OutputPrimary metricWatch out for
Label, action, entity, numberNormalised exact matchExtraction failures; missing aliases
Extracted spanToken F1 (max over golds)Negations and order ignored
JSON / structuredSchema validity rate + per-field accuracy, field F1Averages hiding a critical field; invented fields
CodeUnit tests in a sandbox; pass@1, pass@k (unbiased)Weak or over-specific tests
SQLExecution result match on several DB statesRight answer by accident
Translation (corpus)Overlap metrics as sanity check + human or judgeSentence-level noise
Summary, explanation, chatRubric: required facts, faithfulness, judged (ev4) and calibrated against humans (ev5)ROUGE and similarity rewarding style
Any score used as a thresholdCalibration: reliability diagram, ECEOverconfident high bins
deep:
Validity at two levels: item and system

A metric can be useful for ranking systems and useless for grading individual outputs, or the reverse. At the system level you ask: across several model versions, does the metric's ranking match human rankings? Averaging over hundreds of items cancels much of the per-item noise, so even a crude metric can rank systems tolerably when they differ a lot. At the item level you ask: for individual outputs, does the metric agree with humans about which are good? BLEU was validated at the system level for translation and was never meant for single sentences. When you validate a metric for your task, report both: a rank correlation (Kendall's tau or Spearman's rho) between metric and human ratings over items, and agreement on the ordering of the versions you actually compare. Use item-level validity when the metric selects outputs for review or rejection, and system-level validity when it gates releases.

Micro and macro averages tell different stories

A micro-average pools all items, or all fields, before computing the metric. A macro-average computes the metric per group (per field, per slice, per class) and then averages the groups. With imbalanced groups they diverge. Micro is dominated by the common cases; macro gives a rare but important group equal say. The choice is a statement about what you value. Dashboards should show the per-group numbers, because both averages can hide a group that has collapsed.

Length is a confounder for almost every metric

Recall-oriented metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore recall) rise with length, because longer outputs contain more of the reference's words. Precision-oriented ones fall. Judges, as ev4 shows, often prefer longer answers. Users usually prefer shorter ones. So any change that alters output length, such as a new model, a prompt tweak or a different temperature, moves metrics for reasons unrelated to quality. Report the length distribution alongside every metric, and when comparing versions with different lengths, check whether the metric difference survives controlling for length, for example by comparing within length buckets.

Composite scores hide trade-offs

Teams like a single number, so they combine accuracy, faithfulness, tone and format into a weighted score. The weights are arbitrary, and a composite can stay flat while one component collapses and another improves. Prefer a small set of gate metrics with individual thresholds, each must-pass, and use composites only for coarse ranking of many candidates. If a composite is required, publish its components next to it.

Binary verdicts versus continuous scores
