t: Synthetic data: generating, filtering and trusting LLM-made eval and training data
sum: Using LLMs to generate eval and training data without fooling yourself: attribute-grid and seed-based generation, perturbing real examples, filtering (validity, dedup, quality, answerability), measuring diversity (distinct-n 0.46 vs 1.0 in the worked example), the realism gap that turned 94% synthetic into 71% real, Self-Instruct and phi-1 as training examples, and model collapse with replace versus accumulate.
prereq: ev2
Real traffic is the best source for a golden set; representative and targeted sets are kept apart; contamination means eval items leaking into what the system has seen.
ev4
LLM judges have biases, including preferring outputs that resemble their own; they must be validated against humans.
ev6
Questions generated from a passage reuse its wording, which makes retrieval look easier than it is on real queries.
rs6
Distillation trains a smaller model on outputs (including reasoning traces) generated by a stronger one, often filtered by a verifier.
ae3
Distributions can be compared with histograms and PSI or KL divergence; text is monitored by clustering embeddings into intents or topics.
why:
A team is about to launch an assistant for a new insurance product. There is no production traffic yet, so they ask a strong LLM to generate 2,000 customer questions across the product's features, along with expected answers drawn from the policy documents. Their assistant scores 94% on this set. Two weeks into the beta, an engineer labels 300 real customer questions and the assistant scores 71%. The real questions look nothing like the generated ones. They are fragments ("still no money??"), they combine three issues in one message, they refer to phone calls the assistant knows nothing about, and a fifth of them ask things the policy documents simply don't cover. The synthetic set measured how well the assistant answered questions an LLM imagines customers ask.

Meanwhile, a second team fine-tunes a smaller model on 50,000 synthetic support conversations generated by a larger model, and it works well, until they generate the next round of training data from the fine-tuned model and train on that. Over a few rounds, the model's answers grow more uniform and lose the unusual but correct responses that edge cases need.

Synthetic data, meaning data generated by models rather than collected from people, has become one of the most important tools in AI engineering. It bootstraps eval sets before launch, fills rare slices random sampling never reaches, creates adversarial and perturbed cases, protects privacy where real records can't be used, and supplies training data at a scale no labelling team could. It has also become one of the most common ways teams fool themselves, because synthetic data inherits the biases and blind spots of the model that generated it, and those biases are invisible unless you measure them.

This lesson covers both halves. On the generation side: attribute grids, seeds and perturbations for diverse inputs, verification for generated labels, filtering for validity, duplicates, quality and answerability, and measuring diversity instead of assuming it. On the trust side: the specific ways synthetic data lies (the realism gap, generator bias, label errors, leakage) and how to detect each, with a real anchor set as the cure. Then training data: what Self-Instruct and phi-1 showed about synthetic data done well, and what model collapse shows about synthetic data done recursively, with the replace-versus-accumulate result that says how to avoid it.
primer:
Think of a teacher writing practice exams for their own students. The questions will be useful, covering the syllabus and testing the concepts the teacher emphasised. They will also be shaped by the teacher's mental model: phrased the way the teacher phrases things, focused on what the teacher finds important, and free of the confusions the teacher doesn't know students have. Students who ace the practice exams may still struggle on an exam written by someone else, or on the problems they meet in real life. The practice exam is real practice. It just isn't an unbiased sample of what's coming.

LLM-generated data is a practice exam written by a model. It covers what you ask it to cover, quickly and cheaply, and it reflects the generator's view of the world: its style, its sense of what a typical question looks like, its knowledge and its gaps. The analogy also suggests the remedy. A good teacher checks practice exams against real past papers, and asks colleagues to write some questions. A good team checks synthetic data against real data and uses more than one generator, so that no single model's habits define the whole test.

The synthetic data pipeline

Generation starts from seeds, real examples or hand-written ones, and an attribute grid that spreads generation across the situations you need. Generated items are filtered: invalid ones, duplicates, low-quality ones and unanswerable ones are removed. Generated labels, such as expected answers, are verified, by running code or computing results where possible and by human review of a sample otherwise. The diversity of what survives is measured against real data, because generators repeat themselves. Everything is stored with provenance, marked synthetic, with the generator and prompt recorded. A real anchor set checks the most important property of all: do conclusions drawn from the synthetic data hold on real data?

A rule of thumb helps decide how much of this pipeline a given use needs: the closer synthetic data gets to a decision, the more verification it needs. Synthetic adversarial prompts used to look for weaknesses need little: a strange attack is still a useful test, and a human reviews whatever it finds. Synthetic regression cases that gate a release need verified labels, because a wrong label blocks good releases or passes bad ones. Synthetic data that produces a headline quality number needs to be shown to agree with real data, because executives and customers will act on that number. And synthetic training data needs verification at scale, because errors there are not just mis-scored but learned, and then repeated in every output the trained model produces.

The same pipeline serves training data, with two additions covered later: verifying at much larger scale, usually by rejection sampling against automatic checks, and avoiding the recursive trap that leads to model collapse.
body:
1. Why and when to use synthetic data

Synthetic data earns its place in five situations. Naming which one you're in helps decide how much to trust it.

  • Cold start: no real traffic yet. Synthetic questions let you build a first eval suite before launch. They should be replaced by real traffic as soon as it exists (ev2).
  • Coverage of rare slices: a slice that is 1% of traffic gets few random samples, and generation can produce dozens of cases for it. These belong in targeted suites, not the representative set.
  • Adversarial and edge cases: attacks, boundary conditions, tricky phrasings (ev9). Here synthetic data is the natural source, because real users rarely supply these on demand.
  • Perturbations for robustness: paraphrases, typos, reordered information, irrelevant distractors and changed numbers, generated from real examples. rs8's GSM-Symbolic case showed how templated variants of a benchmark exposed fragility and contamination.
  • Privacy and scale: domains where real records can't be used, such as health or finance, and training data at volumes no human team could label.

In each case synthetic data is a supplement to real data with a specific job. The failure in the opening story was using it as a substitute for the representative set that estimates real quality.

2. Generating inputs that cover the space

Ask an LLM for "1,000 customer questions about returns" and you will get 1,000 variations on a few dozen well-formed questions, because the generator gravitates to its most typical outputs. Diversity has to be engineered. Three techniques work well together.

Attribute grids. Define the dimensions that matter and generate for combinations. For a support assistant: intent (return, delivery, billing, complaint, account, out of scope), persona (first-time buyer, frustrated repeat customer, small-business owner, non-native speaker, elderly user), difficulty (single clear question, multi-issue, ambiguous, unanswerable), style (terse, rambling, typo-heavy, formal), and channel (chat, email, voice transcript). A prompt per combination ("Write a message from a frustrated repeat customer, writing tersely with typos, about a delivery problem that also involves a billing error") produces far more varied inputs than one general prompt. With 6 × 5 × 4 × 4 × 3 = 1,440 combinations, you won't fill every cell. Sample the grid, oversampling cells that matter.

Seeds from real data. Show the generator a few real examples (anonymised) and ask for new ones in the same spirit. This pulls the output toward real phrasing and real concerns, and away from the generator's idea of a typical question. Rotate seeds so the output doesn't cluster around a handful of them.

Perturbing real inputs. Take real examples and transform them. Paraphrase, inject typos, remove punctuation, add irrelevant context ("my daughter's birthday is next week, anyway…"), change numbers and names, switch language, split one message into three. Each perturbation keeps the real example's substance and tests robustness to one kind of variation. For eval purposes, perturbations also give paired comparisons. If a system passes the original and fails the paraphrase, the item is measuring luck (lm14).

For RAG evals there is a specific trap. Generating questions from a document produces questions that reuse the document's words, so retrieval looks unrealistically easy (ev6). Ask the generator to write the question as a user who hasn't read the document would, without using its distinctive terms. Then check lexical overlap between question and source and reject high-overlap items.

3. Generating labels, and verifying them

Generating inputs is relatively safe: a strange input is still a test. Generating expected outputs is riskier, because a wrong label silently grades correct behaviour as wrong, or wrong behaviour as right. And generator errors aren't random. They concentrate in the hard cases, which are exactly where an eval needs to be right.

Verify labels by the strongest available means. For verifiable tasks, check mechanically: run generated code against tests, execute generated SQL, recompute arithmetic, validate extracted fields against a structured source. Generate many candidate answers and keep only those that pass. This is rejection sampling with a verifier, the same idea rs6 described for distilling reasoning. For unverifiable tasks, sample 100-200 items for expert review and measure the label error rate overall and by slice. If 8% of generated labels are wrong, you know scores on this set carry an 8% noise floor (ev5). You can fix labels in risky slices or exclude them. Agreement between two generators from different model families, or across several samples from one, is a cheap flag: items where they disagree go to humans first.

A round-trip check catches a common failure in generated question-answer pairs: questions the context doesn't actually answer. Generate a question from a passage, then have a separate model answer the question from the passage alone, and check the answer matches. Questions that fail are ambiguous, unanswerable or mislabelled. Some should be kept deliberately as unanswerable cases, labelled as such.

4. Filtering

Raw generator output contains a lot of junk, and filtering usually removes a large share of it. A practical filter stack, in order of cost:

  1. Validity: parses, matches the schema, within length limits, in the requested language, not a refusal ("As an AI, I can't…").
  2. Exact duplicates: normalise and hash.
  3. Near-duplicates: items that are trivially different. Use n-gram similarity, MinHash (ev11 works it through), or embedding cosine above a threshold.
  4. Novelty against existing data: remove items too similar to what you already have, including the seeds. Self-Instruct, below, did exactly this for each new instruction.
  5. Quality: a judge scoring realism, correctness and difficulty, validated against human ratings on a sample (ev4). Keep items above a threshold.
  6. Answerability and label checks: round-trip and verification from section 3.
  7. Difficulty: for capability evals, remove items every current system gets right. They add cost without information.
  8. Decontamination: remove anything overlapping your held-out eval sets, so synthetic training data doesn't leak test items (ev2, ev11).

Filters shape the data, so audit them. An LLM quality judge that prefers longer, more formal items will remove exactly the terse, messy inputs real users send. Look at a sample of what each filter removes, not just what it keeps.

5. Self-Instruct: a generation pipeline, worked

Self-Instruct (Wang et al., 2022) is a clear public example of a generate-filter-train pipeline. It started from 175 human-written seed tasks, each an instruction with an example. In each round, it sampled some existing tasks into a prompt and asked GPT-3 to write new instructions. It decided whether each new instruction was a classification task, which affects how instances should be generated, and generated input-output instances for it. Then it filtered: new instructions too similar to existing ones (by ROUGE-L overlap) were discarded, as were invalid or duplicate instances. Survivors joined the pool and seeded later rounds. The result was a dataset of tens of thousands of instructions. Fine-tuning GPT-3 on it gave a 33-point absolute improvement on the Super-NaturalInstructions benchmark, roughly matching InstructGPT-001 there. In human evaluation, the authors report it beat models tuned on existing public instruction datasets by a large margin and came within 5 points of InstructGPT-001.

Three lessons generalise. First, a small, high-quality seed set can bootstrap a large dataset. Second, the novelty filter is what stops the pool collapsing onto a few task types, since without it generation drifts towards its favourites. Third, the result inherits the generator's ceiling. The fine-tuned model approached, but did not exceed, the instruction-following of a model trained with human data. Synthetic data transfers capability; it rarely creates more than the generator has.

6. Measuring diversity

Diversity has to be measured, because generated data that looks varied at a glance often isn't. Four measures, from simplest to most informative:

Distinct-n is the number of unique n-grams across the dataset divided by the total number of n-grams. Worked with four synthetic questions:

  • "how do i return an item i bought"
  • "how do i return a jacket i bought"
  • "how do i return an item i ordered"
  • "how can i return an item i bought"

Each has 8 words and so 7 bigrams, 28 in total. Most repeat ("how do", "do i", "i return", "return an", "an item", "item i", "i bought"), and only 13 are distinct, so distinct-2 = 13/28 = 0.46. Four real messages from the same intent:

  • "jacket doesnt fit can i send it back"
  • "return label never arrived??"
  • "wrong size again, refund pls"
  • "how do i return an item i bought"

These have 7 + 3 + 4 + 7 = 21 bigrams, all distinct, so distinct-2 = 21/21 = 1.0. Distinct-n is crude. It depends on length and ignores meaning, but it catches lazy generation instantly.

Embedding spread: the mean pairwise cosine similarity between items' embeddings, lower meaning more spread. If synthetic items average 0.62 similarity and real items 0.41, the synthetic set is more homogeneous in meaning, not just wording.

Grid coverage: what fraction of attribute-grid cells have at least k surviving items after filtering? Filtering often empties exactly the difficult cells.

Distributional comparison with real data: embed real and synthetic items together, cluster them, and compare the share of each in every cluster. Use PSI or KL divergence from ae3 as a single number, but mainly look for clusters that are real-only (situations the generator never produces) and synthetic-only (situations users never create).

7. When synthetic data lies to you

Synthetic data misleads in recognisable ways. Each has a detection method.

The realism gap. Generated inputs are cleaner, more grammatical, more self-contained, more answerable and more polite than real ones. Systems score higher on them. The opening story's 94% against 71% is typical in direction, if not in size. Detect it by comparing per-slice results on a real anchor set and by the cluster comparison above. In that story, the cluster comparison would show synthetic data almost devoid of multi-issue, context-dependent and unanswerable messages, and the per-slice comparison would show those slices carrying most of the real failures.

Generator bias. The generator writes questions it finds natural and, often, questions it can answer. Systems built on similar models then do unusually well, because the questions sit in their comfort zone. If a judge from the same family grades the outputs, the bias compounds through self-preference (ev4). Detect it by generating with two model families and checking whether system rankings change with the generator, and by cross-family judging.

Label errors. Generated expected answers are wrong at some rate, concentrated in hard cases. Detect it by expert review of a sample (section 3).

Leakage. A generator trained on public benchmarks can reproduce their items or close paraphrases. Generated "fresh" test questions may be contaminated for any model that saw the same benchmarks. Detect it with n-gram and embedding overlap checks against known benchmarks and your own eval sets.

Circularity. Generating data, training on it, and evaluating on more data from the same generator measures agreement with the generator, not quality. Detect it by evaluating on data the generator didn't produce.

The common remedy is a real anchor set: a real-data subset that every synthetic-based evaluation must agree with. The test of a synthetic eval isn't whether its absolute scores match real scores. They usually won't. The test is whether it ranks system versions the same way and shows the same direction of change. Concretely, over the last several system changes, compare the deltas on the synthetic set with the deltas on the anchor. If they agree in sign and roughly in size, the synthetic set is a useful instrument. If they don't, it is measuring something else.

8. Synthetic training data

Synthetic data for training follows the same principles at larger scale, with verification even more important, because errors are learned rather than just mis-scored.

Distillation trains a model on a stronger model's outputs: instructions and responses, reasoning traces, or preferences. rs6 covered distilling reasoning, where generated solutions are filtered by checking final answers, which is rejection sampling with a verifier. Instruction data bootstrapped à la Self-Instruct taught early open models to follow instructions. Curated synthetic corpora can teach specific skills efficiently. The phi-1 paper ("Textbooks Are All You Need", Gunasekar et al., 2023) trained a 1.3B-parameter code model, in four days on eight A100 GPUs, on about 6B tokens of web data filtered for "textbook quality" plus about 1B tokens of synthetic textbooks and exercises generated with GPT-3.5. It reached 50.6% pass@1 on HumanEval and 55.5% on MBPP, competitive at the time with open models many times its size. The lesson is not that synthetic data beats real data. It is that carefully targeted and filtered data, synthetic and real, can be far more valuable per token than raw scale.

Two cautions specific to training. First, check the generator's terms of use. Some providers restrict using their outputs to train competing models. Second, beware the recursion in the next section.

9. Model collapse: replace versus accumulate

Model collapse (Shumailov et al., published in Nature in 2024 under the title "AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data") is what happens when models are trained, generation after generation, on data produced by earlier models. Each generation learns the distribution from a finite sample of the previous model's outputs. Rare events are under-represented in any finite sample, so the next model assigns them less probability, the next sample contains even fewer, and so on. The tails of the distribution, the unusual but valid cases, disappear first. Eventually outputs become narrow and repetitive. The authors demonstrated this in Gaussian mixture models, variational autoencoders and language models, and warned that as the web fills with model-generated text, genuine human data will become increasingly valuable.

A toy simulation shows the mechanism. Start with 100 samples from a standard normal distribution (mean 0, standard deviation 1). Each generation, fit a normal distribution to the current data and draw 100 new samples from the fit.

  • Replace: each generation trains only on the previous generation's samples. In three runs, the fitted standard deviation after 50 generations was about 0.64, 0.33 and 0.45, and after 200 generations about 0.02-0.07. The distribution collapsed to a near-point. The probability of a value beyond ±2, which is 4.6% for the original distribution, falls to about 1.2% at standard deviation 0.8 and to essentially zero by 0.5. The tails go first.
  • Accumulate: each generation's samples are added to a pool that still contains the original 100 real samples, and the fit uses the whole pool. The standard deviation stayed near 1.0 (about 0.91-1.04) for all 200 generations.

That second result matches the theory. Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) showed that replacing real data with each generation's synthetic data tends towards collapse, but accumulating successive generations of synthetic data alongside the original real data avoids it. In the accumulate setting, test error has a finite upper bound independent of the number of iterations. They confirmed this across language models, diffusion models for molecules and variational autoencoders.

The practical rules follow directly. Keep real data in every training mixture and every eval set. Track provenance so you know what is synthetic. Never build a pipeline where a model's outputs become the main training data for its successor without real-data anchoring. And value fresh human data, such as real user interactions (with consent) and expert-written examples, as the scarce resource it is becoming.
deep:
Precision and recall for generated distributions

"Is this synthetic data good?" splits into two questions. Is each generated item realistic, meaning it lies within the support of the real distribution? That is precision. Does the generated set cover all the kinds of real items, including the rare ones? That is recall. Researchers measure these for generative models by checking, in an embedding space, whether each generated item falls near some real item and whether each real item has some generated item nearby. A generator with high precision and low recall produces realistic but narrow data, the typical LLM failure. One with low precision produces varied nonsense. The cluster comparison in the body is a coarse, practical version of the same idea.

Active generation targeted at failures

The most valuable synthetic data is often generated around failures. Take each production failure, characterise what made it hard (a negation, a mixed intent, an unusual unit), and generate variants that share that property. This turns one failure into a family of regression cases and probes whether the fix generalises. It is the eval equivalent of hard-negative mining, and it is how synthetic data helps most at the boundary of what a system can do, which is where random generation is weakest.

Persona prompting has limits

Asking a model to write "as a 70-year-old non-native speaker" produces the generator's stereotype of that person, not a sample of real people. Persona-conditioned data can exaggerate some traits, sanitise others, and encode biases about groups. It is useful for spreading coverage. It is not a substitute for real users from those groups, and evaluation conclusions about how a system serves a group should rest on real data from that group.

Privacy: synthetic is not automatically anonymous

If a generator is fine-tuned on private records, or prompted with them, it can reproduce identifying fragments. A synthetic record that closely mirrors a real one can re-identify the person. Privacy-preserving synthesis needs either generation without access to the records, formal guarantees such as differential privacy in the generator's training, or explicit checks for memorised content (nearest-neighbour distance between synthetic and real records). Treat "it's synthetic, so it's safe" as a claim to verify.

Synthetic preference data and AI feedback

Preference data for alignment can also be synthesised: a model compares two responses against written principles and the preferences train a reward model. This is the idea behind reinforcement learning from AI feedback and constitution-guided approaches. It scales cheaply, and it inherits every judge bias from ev4, including verbosity and self-preference. As with any judge, validate AI preferences against human preferences on a sample, and watch for the trained model drifting towards what the AI judge likes rather than what people do.

Difficulty is a moving target

Synthetic capability evals have a short shelf life. A generator asked for "hard" questions produces questions hard for models like itself at the time; within a model generation or two they are easy, and the eval saturates (ev1). Some teams generate difficulty adaptively: keep the items current systems fail, generate variants of those, and discard items everything passes, so the set tracks the frontier of what the system can do. This keeps the eval informative but makes scores incomparable over time, because the set keeps changing; pair it with a fixed anchor subset for trend lines, as ev2 recommends for any evolving golden set.

Mixing synthetic and real data in one metric

When a single number must combine real and synthetic items, treat them as strata (ev2) and weight each by what it represents, rather than pooling raw counts. A suite of 300 real items and 2,000 synthetic ones, pooled, is 87% synthetic and reports mostly on the generator's world. Reporting the two separately, with the real result as the headline and the synthetic result as coverage, is almost always clearer, and it makes divergence between them visible instead of averaging it away.

Verifiers make synthetic data trustworthy

The domains where synthetic training data works best (maths, code, formal reasoning, structured extraction) share one property: answers can be checked automatically. A verifier turns an untrustworthy generator into a trustworthy data source by rejecting wrong outputs. Where no verifier exists, the quality of synthetic data is bounded by the quality of whatever judges it. So when planning synthetic data, a senior engineer's first question is "what checks each item?", and if the answer is "nothing", a sample-and-measure plan is required before the data is used.
prod:
The public cases: Self-Instruct, phi-1 and model collapse

Three published results together mark out the useful territory for synthetic data. Self-Instruct (Wang et al., 2022) showed that a model could bootstrap its own instruction-following data from 175 seed tasks, with filtering for validity and novelty. Fine-tuning GPT-3 on it gave a 33-point absolute gain on Super-NaturalInstructions, roughly matching InstructGPT-001 there and coming within 5 points of it in human evaluation. The recipe, seed, generate, filter, train, became the template for many open instruction datasets. Its ceiling was the generator's own ability.

phi-1 (Gunasekar et al., 2023) showed that targeted, filtered data, including about 1B tokens of synthetic textbooks and exercises from GPT-3.5 alongside about 6B tokens of filtered web data, could train a 1.3B-parameter model to 50.6% on HumanEval. It is evidence that data quality, of which synthetic generation is one lever, can substitute for a great deal of scale.

Model collapse (Shumailov et al., Nature, 2024; Gerstgrasser et al., 2024) marked the boundary. Recursive training that replaces real data with generated data loses the tails and degrades. Accumulation with real data keeps error bounded. Synthetic data is a powerful complement to real data and a dangerous replacement for it.

Failure modes in practice

The synthetic headline. A team reported "94% accuracy" from a synthetic eval in a launch review. Real-traffic accuracy turned out to be 71%. Fix: headline numbers only from real or realistic representative sets. Synthetic suites are reported separately as coverage and regression results.

The homogeneous set. A synthetic RAG eval of 5,000 questions had a distinct-2 of 0.18 and mean pairwise embedding similarity of 0.7. In effect it held a few hundred questions in many phrasings, all using the documents' own terms. Fix: attribute grids, real seeds, overlap rejection and diversity metrics as acceptance criteria for the set.

The label drift. A model generated expected answers for 3,000 policy questions. A later audit found 11% wrong, concentrated in edge cases, and the team had spent a month "fixing" correct system behaviour to match wrong labels. Fix: verify a sample before use, measure the error rate, and keep provenance so the generated labels can be found and corrected.

The self-referential loop. Training data generated by model A, evaluated on synthetic questions from model A, judged by model A. Every number looked great, and real users disagreed. Fix: different generators and judges for training and evaluation, plus a real anchor.

Synthetic data in the index. A team generated FAQ articles with an LLM to fill gaps in a help centre, and the RAG assistant began answering from them. Some contained confident errors, which the assistant then repeated faithfully. Fix: synthetic content intended for retrieval goes through the same human review as any published documentation, and its provenance is visible to the eval.

What to track

For every dataset with synthetic content, record and display: the synthetic share; the generator models and prompts; filter pass rates per stage; the measured label error rate from the last audit; diversity metrics (distinct-n, embedding spread, grid coverage); the cluster comparison against recent real traffic; and the agreement between synthetic and real anchor results on recent system changes.
myths: Synthetic eval data is a cheap substitute for real data.

It is a supplement with known biases: generated inputs are cleaner, more grammatical, more answerable and less varied than what users send, and the generator's blind spots become the eval's blind spots. In the worked example a system scored 94% on 2,000 synthetic questions and 71% on 300 real ones. Use synthetic data to fill coverage gaps and stress-test, and validate it against a real anchor set.
More synthetic examples means better coverage.

Generators repeat themselves. Without deliberate diversity (attribute grids, personas, seeds from real data) and deduplication, 10,000 generated questions may contain a few hundred distinct situations phrased slightly differently. Coverage is measured, with distinct-n, embedding spread and cluster coverage, not assumed from the count.
If a strong model generated the expected answers, they're correct.

Generated labels carry the generator's errors, and those errors are systematic, concentrated in exactly the hard cases an eval most needs. For verifiable tasks, check labels by execution or computation; for others, have humans verify a sample and measure the error rate before using the labels to grade anything.
Model collapse means you can never train on synthetic data.

Collapse appears when each model generation is trained mainly on the previous generation's outputs, replacing real data: the tails of the distribution shrink and vanish. When synthetic data is added alongside the original real data, rather than replacing it, Gerstgrasser et al. showed test error stays bounded. Many successful models use synthetic data heavily, with filtering and a real-data anchor.
Synthetic data is automatically privacy-safe.

A generator fine-tuned on or prompted with private data can reproduce pieces of it, and a synthetic record built to mirror a real customer can still identify them. Synthetic data reduces privacy risk only when it is generated without access to the private records or checked for memorised content.
lab:
Goal: generate template-based synthetic questions, measure their diversity against a small "real" set, and simulate model collapse. Python 3.12, standard library only. (No LLM is needed: templates stand in for the generator.)

  1. In ev10_lab.py, write 10 short "real" support messages by hand, messy and varied, including one multi-issue and one unanswerable.
  2. Build a "generator": a few templates ("How do I {verb} my {item}?", "Can I {verb} a {item} I {past}?") filled from small word lists, plus an attribute grid (intent × style). For the "terse" style, drop words. For "typo", swap adjacent letters at random. Generate 200 items with random.Random(0).
  3. Write distinct_n(texts, n) and compute distinct-1 and distinct-2 for the real set, for a 10-item sample of the synthetic set, and for the full synthetic set. Reproduce the body's 0.46 and 1.0 on its two four-item examples.
  4. Deduplicate the synthetic set with exact matching after normalisation, then with word-set Jaccard similarity above 0.8. Report how many survive each step.
  5. Model collapse: implement the toy Gaussian simulation from the body. Use 100 samples per generation for 200 generations, with "replace" and "accumulate" modes. Print the fitted standard deviation at generations 1, 10, 50, 100 and 200 for three seeds, and the estimated probability of |x| > 2 at each.

What to look for. The full synthetic set's distinct-2 is far below the real set's even after the style perturbations, and near-duplicate removal shrinks it sharply. That is generation repeating itself. In the collapse simulation, "replace" drives the standard deviation towards zero and the tail probability to nothing within 100-200 generations, at a different speed for each seed. "Accumulate" holds near 1.0. Try keeping only 10% of the original data in the replace pool to see partial anchoring.
recap: Synthetic data, generated by LLMs, fills gaps where real data is missing: cold-start eval sets, rare and adversarial slices, privacy-sensitive domains, and training data at scale.

Diverse generation needs structure: an attribute grid (intent × persona × difficulty × language × style), seeds from real examples, and perturbations of real inputs (paraphrases, typos, distractors, changed numbers).
Generated expected outputs must be verified: by execution or computation for verifiable tasks, otherwise by human review of a sample with a measured error rate.

Filtering removes invalid, duplicate, low-quality, unanswerable and trivially easy items; Self-Instruct filtered generated instructions by similarity to existing ones before fine-tuning GPT-3 on them, gaining 33 points on Super-NaturalInstructions.

Measure diversity rather than assume it: in the worked example four synthetic questions had distinct-2 of 13/28 = 0.46 against 1.0 for four real ones; compare cluster distributions with real traffic too.

Synthetic data lies through the realism gap (clean, answerable inputs), generator bias (its blind spots and style), label errors and leakage; validate by checking that system rankings on synthetic data match rankings on a real anchor set.

Synthetic training data works when filtered and grounded: phi-1 (1.3B parameters) used 6B tokens of filtered web 'textbook-quality' data plus 1B synthetic tokens from GPT-3.5 and reached 50.6% pass@1 on HumanEval.

Model collapse: training each generation only on the previous generation's outputs makes the tails disappear (a toy Gaussian refit shrank its standard deviation from 1.0 to under 0.1 in 200 generations), while accumulating synthetic data alongside real data keeps error bounded.
Label provenance (real or synthetic, which generator, which prompt), cap synthetic shares in headline evals, and keep a real-data anchor in every set.
glossary: Answerability check
Verifying that a generated question can actually be answered from the given context, for example by having a model answer it and checking the answer.
Attribute grid
A set of dimensions (intent, persona, difficulty, language, style) whose combinations are used to steer generation toward coverage.
Distillation
Training a model on outputs generated by another, usually stronger, model.
Distinct-n
The number of unique n-grams in a set of texts divided by the total number of n-grams; a simple measure of lexical diversity.
Generator bias
Systematic tendencies of the model producing synthetic data (its style, topics, blind spots) that carry into the data.
Model collapse
Degradation of models trained recursively on generated data, in which rare events (the tails of the distribution) disappear first.
Perturbation
Creating new examples by modifying real ones: paraphrasing, adding typos or distractors, changing numbers or names.
Persona conditioning
Prompting a generator to write as a specific kind of user (a hurried novice, an angry customer, a non-native speaker) to diversify inputs.
Provenance
The record of where an example came from: real traffic, which generator and prompt, which filters it passed.
Realism gap
The systematic differences between synthetic and real inputs, such as cleaner language, clearer intent and higher answerability.
Rejection sampling
Generating many candidates and keeping only those that pass a check (tests, a verifier, a judge).
Round-trip check
Generating data in one direction and checking it in the other, such as generating a question from a passage and checking that the passage answers it.
Seed example
A real or hand-written example used to prompt a generator to produce similar but new examples.
Self-Instruct
A method for bootstrapping instruction-tuning data by having a model generate new tasks and examples from a small seed set, with filtering.
Synthetic data
Data generated by models rather than collected from real users or written by people.
Anchor set
A real-data subset kept in every evaluation to check that synthetic results agree with reality.
drill:
Design and diagnose: a synthetic eval for a new feature

Your team is launching a "chat with your bank statements" feature in six weeks. You can't use real customer statements for evaluation before launch. A colleague proposes generating 3,000 synthetic statements with an LLM, generating 5 questions per statement with the same LLM, generating expected answers with it too, and gating launch at 90% accuracy. Critique the plan and propose a better one.

Answer

Problems with the plan. (1) Circularity: the same model generates the data, the questions and the answers, so the eval measures agreement with that model. (2) Label errors: statement questions are numeric ("how much did I spend on groceries in March?"), and LLMs make arithmetic and aggregation errors, which concentrate in exactly the multi-step questions that matter. (3) Realism gap: generated statements will be cleaner than real ones (consistent merchant names, no pending transactions, no refunds, no currency conversions), and generated questions cleaner than users' ("why is my money gone", "that coffee place thing"). (4) Clustering: 5 questions per statement means effective sample size well below 15,000 (ev7). (5) A 90% gate on synthetic data says little about real accuracy.

Better plan. Generate statements programmatically, not with an LLM. Use a simulator with realistic merchant-name variation, pending and reversed transactions, refunds, foreign currency, recurring payments, and statistics drawn from published or internal aggregate spending patterns. Then the ground truth is computed exactly by code: answers are verified by construction.

Questions. Write 100 by hand with the product team and support staff, in real users' voice. Collect phrasing from existing support tickets about statements, without personal data. Then generate variants with two different model families using an attribute grid: question type (sum, find, compare, explain, unanswerable), time reference style, vagueness, typos. Expected answers come from code over the simulated statement, never from the LLM.

Filtering and diversity. Deduplicate. Check that each question's computed answer is unique, flagging ambiguous ones. Measure distinct-n and the grid coverage. Include 15% unanswerable or ambiguous questions where the expected behaviour is to ask or decline.

Anchor. Run an internal dogfood: employees use the feature on their own statements with consent and rate answers. That gives a small real anchor. Check that system changes move dogfood and synthetic results in the same direction.

Gate. Set separate thresholds per question type, with intervals computed at the statement level. Ship to a small beta, and replace synthetic headline numbers with real-traffic labels as soon as possible.
qa: M
How do you use synthetic perturbations to test robustness, and how do you analyse the results?

Take real items and apply controlled transformations one at a time (paraphrase, typos, irrelevant context, reordered facts, changed numbers or names), keeping the expected answer fixed or updating it by rule. Run the system on originals and variants and analyse them as pairs: the share of items that pass the original but fail a variant measures fragility to that transformation, with intervals from a paired analysis (ev7). Large drops point to specific weaknesses, as GSM-Symbolic showed when one irrelevant clause cut some models' accuracy sharply.

Follow-up: Why perturb real items rather than generate new ones? — Because the comparison is paired: everything except the one transformation is held constant, so a change in outcome is attributable to that transformation.
E
When is synthetic data useful for evaluation?

When real data is missing or insufficient: before launch (cold start), for rare slices that random sampling barely covers, for adversarial and edge cases, for privacy-sensitive domains where you can't use real records, and for perturbations that test robustness (paraphrases, typos, distractors). It's a supplement: the headline estimate of quality should still come from real or realistic data.
E
How do you make generated eval questions diverse?

Give the generator structure: an attribute grid (intent, persona, difficulty, language, writing style, length) and generate for each combination; seed with real examples and ask for variations; perturb real inputs; vary the generator model and temperature. Then deduplicate and measure diversity (distinct-n, embedding spread, cluster coverage) against real traffic.
E
What is model collapse?

Degradation that happens when models are trained recursively on data generated by earlier models. Each generation estimates the distribution from a finite sample of the previous model's outputs, rare events are under-sampled and drop out, and over generations the tails vanish and outputs become narrower and less diverse. Shumailov et al. showed it for Gaussian mixtures, VAEs and language models; keeping real data in the mix and accumulating rather than replacing data prevents it.
M
Your synthetic eval says 94%; on 300 real questions the system scores 71%. Explain and fix.

The realism gap. Generated questions are cleaner, single-intent, well-specified and answerable; real users write fragments, mix intents, refer to context, misspell and ask unanswerable things. If the generator wrote questions from the documents, they also share the documents' wording, which flatters retrieval. Compare slices: the gap is usually largest on messy, ambiguous or out-of-scope inputs. Fix by seeding generation with real examples, adding persona and style conditioning, perturbing toward real noise, including unanswerable questions, and keeping the real set as the anchor that the synthetic one must track.
Follow-up: How do you know the synthetic set is now good enough? — Check that it ranks system versions the same way the real set does across several changes, and that the per-slice gaps are small.
M
How do you verify labels or expected answers generated by an LLM?

For verifiable tasks, verify mechanically: run code against tests, execute SQL, compute the arithmetic, check a fact against a structured source. For others, sample 100-200 items for expert review, measure the label error rate overall and by slice, and either fix the labels, filter the risky slices, or only use the set for purposes that tolerate that error. Also use agreement between independent generators or multiple samples as a flag for uncertain labels, and route those to humans.
M
Walk through a filtering pipeline for generated training examples.

Validity: parse, schema, length limits, language. Deduplication: exact hashes, then near-duplicates by MinHash or embedding similarity (Self-Instruct filtered new instructions too similar to existing ones). Quality: a validated judge scoring correctness, helpfulness and instruction-following, keeping the top share. Verification: execution or tests where possible, rejection sampling with a verifier. Decontamination: remove anything overlapping eval sets. Difficulty: drop items every model already gets right if the goal is improvement. Then sample the survivors for human review.

Follow-up: What's the risk in filtering with an LLM judge? — The judge's biases shape the data (length, style, its own preferences), so the trained model inherits them; validate the judge and audit what the filter removes.
M
How do you measure the diversity of a synthetic dataset?

Lexically with distinct-n (unique n-grams over total); semantically with mean pairwise embedding similarity or the spread of embeddings; structurally with coverage of your attribute grid; and distributionally by clustering real and synthetic data together and comparing cluster proportions, for example with PSI or KL divergence. In my small example, four synthetic paraphrases had distinct-2 of 0.46 against 1.0 for four real messages; cluster comparison shows which real intents the synthetic set misses.
Follow-up: Can a dataset be too diverse? — Yes, if diversity comes from unrealistic inputs; diversity should match the real distribution's spread, not exceed it with things users never do.
M
What did Self-Instruct do, and what does it teach about synthetic data?

It started from 175 human-written seed tasks, prompted GPT-3 to generate new instructions, inputs and outputs, filtered out invalid ones and ones too similar to existing tasks, and fine-tuned GPT-3 on the result. That gave a 33-point absolute improvement on Super-NaturalInstructions, roughly matching InstructGPT-001 there. The lessons: a small seed set can bootstrap a large dataset, filtering for validity and novelty is essential, and the result inherits the generator's quality ceiling and style.
H
When does synthetic data lie to you, and how do you detect each case?

Realism gap: detect by comparing slice results and cluster distributions against real data. Generator bias: the data reflects what the generator finds easy and natural, so systems similar to the generator score well; detect by checking whether rankings shift when you swap generators. Label errors: systematic in hard cases; detect by expert review of a sample. Leakage: the generator may reproduce benchmark or eval content it saw in training; detect by overlap checks. Circularity: grading synthetic outputs with a judge from the same family; detect by cross-family judging. The common remedy is a real anchor set and checks that synthetic and real agree on rankings.
Follow-up: What's the single most important safeguard? — Never let synthetic data be the only evidence for a decision; require that conclusions hold on a real subset.
H
Explain the replace-versus-accumulate distinction in model collapse.

If each generation trains only on the previous model's outputs, replacing the real data, estimation errors compound: rare events are under-represented in each finite sample, the next model assigns them even less probability, and the tails disappear, as in Shumailov et al. If each generation's synthetic data is added to a pool that still contains the original real data, the real data keeps anchoring the distribution, and Gerstgrasser et al. proved test error has a finite upper bound independent of the number of iterations. In a toy Gaussian simulation, replacing shrank the standard deviation from 1.0 to under 0.1 in 200 generations while accumulating held it near 1.0.

Follow-up: Why does this matter for web-scale pretraining? — An increasing share of web text is model-generated; data pipelines that can't distinguish it risk drifting towards replacement, which is why provenance, filtering and preserved human data matter.
H
Design a synthetic data strategy for evaluating a new insurance-claims assistant with no production traffic.

Start with real material: anonymised historic claims conversations from human agents, policy documents, and 50 questions written by claims handlers. Define an attribute grid: claim type, policy type, customer persona (first-time, frustrated, non-native speaker), difficulty, channel style, plus unanswerable and out-of-scope cases. Generate with two different model families, seeded with the real examples, with instructions to include realistic noise. Filter for validity and duplicates, check answerability against documents, and have claims handlers verify expected outcomes on a 20% sample, measuring label error. Measure diversity against the historic conversations. Label provenance. Use the synthetic set for coverage and regression, the handler-written and historic sets as the anchor, and replace synthetic with real traffic as soon as the beta produces it.

Follow-up: How would you know when to retire synthetic items? — When real traffic provides enough examples in a slice, compare results; if they agree, keep the synthetic items as regression cases but stop using them for headline estimates.

Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model with further training on task data, either all weights or small adapters (LoRA, QLoRA); a few thousand good examples can change behaviour substantially.
ev2
Eval items leaking into training data contaminate the eval; the GPT-3 paper used 13-word overlaps for benchmark decontamination.
ev10

why:
A company fine-tunes a model on two years of its customer-support conversations, about 400,000 of them, to make an assistant that writes like its best agents. The first version has strange habits. It ends a third of its replies with the same sign-off paragraph, word for word. It recommends a discontinued product. On one internal test, it reproduces a real customer's phone number. Its evaluation scores are excellent, suspiciously so on a few questions it answers with uncanny precision.

Every one of these problems was in the data. The repeated sign-off came from a support macro pasted into 60,000 conversations, so the model learned it as the most important thing to say. The discontinued product came from old conversations nobody filtered by date. The phone number appeared in dozens of conversations with one persistent customer and was memorised. The uncanny eval answers were memorised too: some eval questions had come from the same support logs and were sitting in the training data.

Fine-tuning (lm11) is often described as "train on your data". The hard part is deciding what your data should be. That job is data curation: sourcing, cleaning, deduplicating, filtering for quality, deciding the mixture, removing anything that overlaps the evals, handling personal data, and knowing where every example came from and whether you're allowed to use it. It is unglamorous work that decides more about the resulting model than most modelling choices. It is also an evaluation problem in two senses. Every curation step should be justified by evals of the trained model, and curation done wrong, through contamination, makes those evals meaningless.

This lesson walks the pipeline. It covers cleaning and normalisation, exact deduplication, and near-duplicate detection with MinHash, worked by hand on two sentences, with the banding trick that makes it scale, using the configuration from the FineWeb web dataset. It covers heuristic and model-based quality filters, mixtures and epochs, decontamination against eval sets, PII detection and masking, and licensing and provenance. The case is the 2021 paper that showed how much duplication standard training sets contain and what removing it does.
primer:
Curating training data is like editing an anthology. You have a mountain of submissions. Many are near-copies of each other: the same story submitted twice with a new title, three versions with minor edits. Some are badly written, some are off-topic, some infringe someone's copyright, and some contain a real person's private details. A few are the very stories the critics will use to review the anthology, and including them would be cheating. The editor's job is to choose, from the mountain, a collection that teaches readers what the anthology is meant to teach, in the right proportions, with each piece included once, legally and safely.

The analogy breaks in scale. An editor reads every submission, and can tell at a glance that two stories are the same one retitled. A training pipeline may handle millions of documents and can't compare every pair for near-duplication, since that would be trillions of comparisons. Much of the technical content of curation is about doing an editor's judgement automatically, cheaply and measurably at that scale, and about checking afterwards, with evals of the trained model, that the automated judgement was right.

The curation funnel

Each stage of the funnel targets one problem. Cleaning removes what isn't usable at all: broken records, the wrong language, data outside the relevant period. Exact deduplication removes identical copies. Near-duplicate removal collapses templated and lightly edited copies, which is where most real duplication lives. Quality filtering keeps examples worth imitating. Decontamination removes anything overlapping the eval sets. PII masking and licence checks make the data safe and legal to use. The output is a versioned dataset with a datasheet describing all of the above.

Why does each stage matter enough to justify its cost? Because a model learns whatever is frequent and consistent in its data, whether you meant it to or not. Duplicates make a few examples frequent, so the model over-learns them, and that is how a support macro becomes a verbal tic or a phone number becomes a memorised string. Low-quality examples are consistent in their flaws, so the model learns the flaws. Eval items in training make the model look like it generalises when it remembers. Personal data that appears often enough can be reproduced word for word. Every stage of the funnel removes one way the data could teach the wrong lesson, and the order matters too: cheap, high-volume stages first, so expensive ones such as model-based filters and human review run on less data.

Two further decisions sit across the funnel. The first is the mixture: how much of each source goes into training, and how many times small sources are repeated. The second is validation: every step is a hypothesis ("removing these makes the model better"), and the way to test it is to train with and without the step and compare on the eval suite.
body:
1. Sourcing and cleaning

Fine-tuning data usually comes from four kinds of source, each with characteristic problems. Production logs, such as past support conversations, user-accepted drafts and resolved tickets, are realistic and abundant. They are also full of personal data, templated text and behaviour you don't want to imitate (rude agents, wrong answers, outdated policy), and using them needs a lawful basis and attention to retention rules (ae5). Expert-written examples are high quality and expensive, so there are always few of them. Public datasets are convenient and come with licences and unknown contamination. Synthetic data (ev10) is cheap and scalable, and carries the generator's biases and label errors.

Cleaning makes the data usable. Parse records into the training format (instruction and response, or multi-turn conversations), dropping those that fail to parse. Normalise text: consistent Unicode, whitespace and line endings, and remove markup, signatures and quoted reply chains in emails. Filter by language if the model targets specific languages. Filter by date where content goes stale, such as policies and product names. Remove records whose outcome shows they're bad targets: escalated conversations, replies later corrected by a supervisor, tickets reopened by the customer. Each filter should be logged with how many records it removed, because a filter that removes 40% when you expected 5% is usually a bug.

2. Exact deduplication

The simplest duplicates are identical after normalisation. Normalise (lower-case, collapse whitespace, strip punctuation if appropriate), hash each record with a fast hash, and keep one record per hash. It is cheap, linear in the data size, and catches a surprising amount: repeated submissions, logging bugs that wrote records twice, data merged from overlapping exports.

Duplication can also live at the substring level: a long boilerplate paragraph inside otherwise different documents. Lee et al. (2021) used a suffix array, a sorted list of every suffix of the concatenated corpus, to find repeated substrings of 50 tokens or more and remove them. That is how they found a 61-word English sentence repeated over 60,000 times in C4 (the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus), a widely used web corpus. For fine-tuning data, the equivalent is the repeated sign-off macro from the opening story. Removing it from the training targets, while keeping the conversations, solves the problem.

3. Near-duplicates and Jaccard similarity

Most duplication is near-duplication: the same support macro with a different customer name, the same article with different navigation text, the same template with a changed number. Exact hashing misses all of it, because one changed character changes the hash completely. To find near-duplicates we need a similarity measure and a way to compute it at scale.

The standard measure is Jaccard similarity between sets of shingles. A shingle is an overlapping sequence of n words (or characters), and a document is represented as the set of its shingles. Jaccard similarity is J(A, B) = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|.

Worked, with word bigrams (n = 2) on two support sentences that differ by one word:

  • A: "refunds are processed within five business days of approval"
  • B: "refunds are processed within seven business days of approval"

Each has 9 words and so 8 bigrams. Number the distinct bigrams across both: 0 "refunds are", 1 "are processed", 2 "processed within", 3 "within five", 4 "five business", 5 "business days", 6 "days of", 7 "of approval", 8 "within seven", 9 "seven business". Then A = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7} and B = {0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9}. They share 6 bigrams (0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7), and their union has 10. So J = 6/10 = 0.6.

One changed word removed two shared bigrams from each side, because every shingle containing that word differs. In a 300-word document, the same one-word change would leave Jaccard near 0.99. Shingle size matters too: larger n makes the measure stricter, since more shingles touch each change. FineWeb used 5-word shingles for web documents.

Computing exact Jaccard for every pair is the problem. With a million documents there are about 5 × 1011 pairs, and each comparison handles sets of hundreds of shingles. MinHash shrinks each document to a short signature, and banding avoids comparing most pairs at all.

4. MinHash, worked by hand

MinHash (Broder, 1997) rests on one observation. Take a random hash function h that assigns each shingle a number, effectively putting all shingles in a random order. Look at the smallest hash value in A and the smallest in B. Consider the union A ∪ B: under a random ordering, its smallest element is equally likely to be any of its members. The two minima are equal exactly when that smallest element is in both sets, which happens with probability |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|. So:

P(min h(A) = min h(B)) = J(A, B)

One hash function gives a yes/no observation with probability J. Use k independent hash functions and the fraction of matching minima estimates J. Each document is represented by its signature, the k minima, and comparing two documents means comparing two short vectors.

Worked with the two sentences and 8 toy hash functions of the form h(x) = (a·x + b) mod 11, applied to the bigram numbers 0-9. Because 11 is prime, each of these functions just reorders the numbers 0-10, which is exactly the random ordering MinHash needs.

Check one row by hand. For (a, b) = (1, 3), bigram 8 ("within seven", only in B) hashes to (8 + 3) mod 11 = 0, the smallest possible value, so B's minimum is 0. A doesn't contain bigram 8, and its smallest value is 3, from bigram 0. The minima differ because the "winner" of the union was a bigram unique to B. In the (3, 1) row, the winner is bigram 7 ("of approval", value (21 + 1) mod 11 = 0), which both sentences contain, so the minima match.

4 of 8 minima match, so the MinHash estimate is 0.5, against a true Jaccard of 0.6. That isn't an error in the method; it's sampling noise. Each hash is a coin flip with probability 0.6, so with k hashes the standard error of the estimate is √(J(1 − J)/k). For k = 8 that is √(0.24/8) ≈ 0.17, so 0.5 is well within one standard error. With k = 128 it falls to about 0.043, and with FineWeb's 112 hashes (14 × 8) to about 0.046. Production systems use around 100 or more hash functions, and can confirm pairs near the threshold with exact Jaccard.

5. Banding: finding candidates without comparing every pair

Signatures make each comparison cheap, but comparing every pair is still quadratic. Locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) avoids most comparisons. Split each signature of k = b × r values into b bands of r consecutive values. For each band, hash its r values into a bucket. Two documents become a candidate pair if they land in the same bucket for at least one band, and only candidate pairs are compared (or simply treated as duplicates).

The probability that two documents with similarity s match on all r values of one band is sr. The probability that they match on at least one of b bands is

P(candidate) = 1 − (1 − sr)b

FineWeb's configuration, from the datatrove pipeline used to build it, is 5-word shingles with 14 bands of 8 hashes each (112 hash functions), applied separately to each Common Crawl dump. Plugging in b = 14 and r = 8:

Similarity ss8P(candidate) = 1 − (1 − s8)14

The curve is S-shaped, with its steep part near (1/b)1/r = (1/14)1/8 ≈ 0.72. Pairs well above that are almost always caught, and pairs well below almost never become candidates. You tune the threshold with b and r: more rows per band make the curve steeper and push the threshold up, more bands push it down. The trade-off is between missed duplicates (false negatives, pairs above the intended threshold that escape) and wasted comparisons or wrong merges (false positives, pairs below it that get caught).

After candidates are found, duplicates are grouped, often by treating candidate pairs as edges and taking connected components, and one representative per group is kept. One finding from FineWeb's ablations is worth knowing: deduplicating each crawl dump separately produced better models than deduplicating across all dumps globally. Aggressive global deduplication had removed proportionally more of the higher-quality content that recurs across crawls, leaving a lower-quality remainder. Even deduplication is a choice to validate with ablations, not a step whose more aggressive version is automatically better.

6. Quality filters

After deduplication, the next question is which examples are worth imitating. There are two kinds of filter.

Heuristic rules are cheap and transparent. Examples are length bounds, the share of non-alphabetic characters, repeated lines or n-grams, language-identification confidence, presence of boilerplate phrases, and for code, whether it parses. Rules like these were used to build large pretraining corpora. DeepMind's Gopher work, for instance, filtered web documents by word count (keeping roughly 50 to 100,000 words) and mean word length, among other rules. For fine-tuning data, domain rules matter more: drop conversations that were escalated, replies later corrected, tickets reopened, and responses that don't follow the current policy.

Model-based filters score each example with a learned model. You can train a small classifier on a few hundred examples labelled good or bad by experts, or use a validated LLM judge (ev4) with a rubric for what makes a good training target. FineWeb-Edu is a public example at scale: an LLM rated a sample of web pages for educational value, a classifier trained on those ratings scored all of FineWeb, and the high-scoring 1.3 trillion tokens became FineWeb-Edu. For fine-tuning on support conversations, outcome signals are often the best "labels": conversations that resolved without follow-up contact and earned good ratings make better targets than ones that merely read fluently.

LIMA (Zhou et al., 2023) showed how far quality can substitute for quantity. A 65B-parameter LLaMA model fine-tuned on just 1,000 carefully curated prompt-response pairs, with no reinforcement learning, produced responses that people judged equivalent to or better than GPT-4's in 43% of comparisons, 58% against Bard and 65% against DaVinci003. The authors' interpretation, which they called the superficial alignment hypothesis, was that almost all knowledge is learned in pretraining and fine-tuning mainly teaches format and style, so a small, excellent dataset suffices for that.

Audit what filters remove, by slice. A classifier trained mostly on English may score other languages lower. A judge that likes long answers removes concise good ones. A rule that drops short conversations may remove all of a quick-resolution intent. Sample the rejected examples, not just the accepted ones.

7. Mixtures and epochs

Fine-tuning data usually comes from several sources of different sizes and value, and the mixture decides how much each contributes. Worked example: 40,000 filtered support conversations (realistic, medium quality), 2,000 expert-written examples (high quality, covering weak areas) and 20,000 verified synthetic examples (rare intents and edge cases). You plan a training set of 30,000 examples with target shares of 50/20/30.

SourceAvailableTarget shareExamples drawnEpochs over source
Support conversations40,00050%15,0000.375 (sampled)
Expert-written2,00020%6,0003 (each repeated 3×)
Synthetic, verified20,00030%9,0000.45

Small, valuable sources are upsampled, repeated over several epochs (passes over that source). Large, noisier ones are down-sampled. Repetition has limits. Each extra pass gives less new signal and raises the risk of memorising those exact examples, so watch held-out performance on that source and test for verbatim regurgitation. The weights themselves are hypotheses to tune with evals per capability. If tone improves but policy accuracy drops, the mixture is over-weighting conversational style relative to policy knowledge. Keep a general-capability eval too, because a narrow mixture can erode skills the base model had, which is sometimes called forgetting.

8. Decontamination

Decontamination removes training examples that overlap evaluation data. It is the training-side half of the contamination problem ev2 raised for golden sets. In the opening story, eval questions taken from the same support logs ended up in the training data, and the model's "uncanny precision" on them was memory. Lee et al. found the same issue in public data: over 4% of the validation sets of some standard datasets overlapped their training sets.

A practical decontamination step:

  1. Normalise training and eval text identically.
  2. N-gram overlap: flag any training example sharing a long run of words with any eval item, such as 13 consecutive words, the threshold the GPT-3 paper used for its benchmark decontamination. Index eval n-grams in a hash set so each training example is checked in one pass.
  3. Semantic overlap: flag training examples whose embedding is very close to an eval item, to catch paraphrases and synthetic variants generated from eval items, which share meaning but few long n-grams.
  4. Review and remove flagged examples, recording what was removed and why. Sometimes the eval item is the one to retire, if it turns out to be a common template that legitimately appears in training.
  5. Re-run whenever the training data or any eval set changes.

Worked: checking 150,400 training examples against 1,200 eval items flags 600 training examples overlapping 41 eval items. Most are a support macro that appears in both. The training examples are removed, leaving 149,800. The 41 eval items are re-examined: 35 stay, since the overlap was a shared policy sentence now removed from training, and 6 are retired from the eval as too templated to test generalisation. Without this step, the evaluation of the fine-tuned model would have overstated quality on exactly those items.

9. PII detection and masking

Production data contains personal information, and fine-tuned models can memorise and reproduce it, especially data that repeats, like the persistent customer's phone number. PII handling combines several detectors:

  • Patterns for structured identifiers: email addresses, phone numbers in local formats, card numbers (validated with the Luhn checksum to cut false positives), national ID formats, IBANs, IP addresses.
  • Named-entity recognition for names, addresses and organisations, which patterns can't catch reliably.
  • Context rules, such as "my account number is …".

Detected PII is replaced with typed placeholders ("[EMAIL]", "[PHONE]"), or with realistic fakes that are consistent within a conversation, so the model still learns the conversational structure without the real values. Where a field isn't needed at all, drop it before detection. Removal by design beats detection.

Measure the detector. Seed a sample with known PII and count how much it finds. Suppose it catches 940 of 1,000 seeded instances, a recall of 94%. If about 3% of 150,000 conversations contain PII, roughly 4,500 conversations, then around 6% of those instances, a couple of hundred, may survive. Whether that is acceptable depends on sensitivity, and it usually argues for layering: dropping fields, deduplication (which removes repeated records, the ones most likely to be memorised), and a memorisation test before release. Prompt the model with prefixes of training records containing masked-then-reinserted canary values, and check whether it completes them verbatim.

10. Licensing and provenance

Every dataset raises the question "are we allowed to use this, for this purpose?" The answer depends on the source. Your own production data depends on your terms of service, privacy policy, consents and retention rules. Public datasets come with licences: permissive ones (MIT, Apache 2.0, CC BY), copyleft or share-alike ones (GPL, CC BY-SA), non-commercial ones (CC BY-NC), and custom terms. Scraped content raises terms-of-service questions, and some publishers signal opt-outs. Model-generated data depends on the provider's terms, some of which restrict using outputs to train competing models. Contractor-written data depends on the contract's ownership terms. This lesson isn't legal advice, and these questions need legal review, but the engineering requirement is clear. Record the source and licence of every dataset, decide deliberately whether each use is permitted, and keep enough lineage to remove a source and retrain if needed.

A datasheet (Gebru et al., 2018) is the standard way to record this. It covers motivation, sources, composition (sizes, languages, slices, synthetic share), collection process, every preprocessing step with its version and thresholds, known gaps and biases, licences, and permitted and prohibited uses. It turns the curation pipeline from tribal knowledge into an auditable artefact, and it is what lets someone answer a question about the model months later.
deep:
Validating curation with ablations

Every curation step is a hypothesis about what makes a better model, and the only real test is training with and without it. Dataset papers like FineWeb are largely collections of such ablations: train small models on data processed different ways, with equal compute, and compare on a fixed suite of evals. For a fine-tuning team, a reduced version is usually affordable: a smaller base model or fewer steps, a few variants (raw, deduplicated, deduplicated plus filtered), paired comparison per capability (ev7), plus memorisation and safety checks. Ablations often overturn intuitions. FineWeb's finding that per-dump deduplication beat global deduplication is a reminder that "more aggressive" is not "better" by default.

Choosing shingle size and threshold

Shingle size and similarity threshold define what counts as a duplicate. Small shingles (unigrams) make unrelated documents on the same topic look similar. Large shingles (10+ words) make lightly edited copies look different. Thresholds that are too low merge distinct documents. Too high, and templated variants survive. The right values depend on document length and on what kind of near-duplication you need to remove: boilerplate-heavy web pages differ from short support replies. Calibrate on a labelled sample. Have people mark a few hundred pairs as duplicate or not, then pick parameters whose LSH curve separates them, measuring precision and recall of the duplicate decision.

Semantic deduplication

MinHash finds lexical near-duplicates. Two support answers that say the same thing in different words are not caught. Semantic deduplication embeds examples and clusters them, keeping a representative subset of each tight cluster. This can remove redundancy that lexical methods miss and, in some reported pretraining experiments, has improved efficiency. It is more expensive and riskier, because embedding similarity also merges examples that differ in exactly the detail that matters (ev3's negation problem). Use it for redundancy reduction in large, homogeneous sources, with careful thresholds and spot checks, not as a replacement for lexical dedup.

Contamination you can't see by overlap

N-gram and embedding checks catch copies and paraphrases. They don't catch a training set that teaches the specific answers to eval questions in a different form, for example a policy explanation written by someone who was looking at the eval set. Nor do they catch data that makes the eval easier for systematic reasons, such as training heavily on the exact templates the eval uses. Organisational controls handle these: separate eval and training data owners, access controls on eval sets, and a rule that nobody writing training data looks at eval items. Fresh eval items written after the training data was frozen are the final check (ev2).

Data poisoning

If training data includes content an adversary can influence, such as scraped web pages, user-submitted feedback or public datasets, an attacker can plant examples that teach a backdoor or a bias. The OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10 for LLM applications lists data and model poisoning for this reason. Curation defences include provenance tracking (knowing which sources could be influenced), anomaly detection on new data, deduplication (poisoning often relies on repetition), and evaluating for specific triggered behaviours. ev9's red-teaming mindset applies to the data pipeline too.

Curation for preference data and evaluation data

The same pipeline applies, with twists, to other kinds of data. Preference data for alignment (pairs of responses with a preferred one) needs deduplication of prompts, so a few prompts don't dominate; filtering of pairs where labellers disagreed (ev5), which carry little signal; and decontamination against evals just like instruction data. Evaluation data needs curation too: golden sets should be deduplicated, because ten near-identical items inflate the apparent sample size and shrink intervals falsely (ev7), and checked for PII before they are shared with vendors or contractors (ev2). A team that builds one curation library and applies it to training, preference and evaluation data avoids maintaining three inconsistent ones.

Recording what was removed

Teams record what they keep and rarely what they discard. Keeping a sample of removed examples per filter, with the reason, makes three things possible. You can audit filter behaviour by slice. You can recover data if a filter turns out to be wrong. And you can answer "why doesn't the model handle X?" when X was filtered out. It costs little storage and saves a great deal of debugging.
prod:
The public case: "Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better" (Lee et al., 2021)

This paper, from researchers at Google, quantified how much duplication standard language-model training sets contain, and what removing it does. The authors built two tools. The first, exact substring deduplication, used a suffix array over the whole corpus to find and remove repeated runs of 50 or more tokens. The second, approximate deduplication, used MinHash with LSH to find near-duplicate documents. Applied to widely used datasets, including C4, the tools found extensive duplication. The most memorable example is a single 61-word English sentence repeated over 60,000 times in C4. Many documents were near-copies, such as templated pages that differed only in a product name or location.

They then trained language models on the original and deduplicated versions. Models trained on deduplicated data emitted memorised training text ten times less often, and reached the same or better accuracy with fewer training steps. They also measured train-test overlap. Over 4% of the validation sets of some standard datasets overlapped their training sets, which means evaluation numbers on those sets had been partly measuring memorisation. They released their code.

The production lessons map directly onto fine-tuning work. Duplication is everywhere, mostly in near-duplicate form, and exact hashing alone misses it. Duplicates cause memorisation, which is a quality problem (repeated macros) and a privacy problem (repeated personal data). And training-evaluation overlap silently inflates scores, so decontamination is part of evaluation, not an optional extra. Later dataset efforts, including FineWeb with its documented MinHash configuration, made these steps standard practice.

Failure modes in practice
