The macro parrot. A fine-tuned support model ended a third of its replies with a sign-off pasted into 60,000 training conversations. Fix: substring-level deduplication of repeated spans in targets, plus near-duplicate collapsing of templated replies.

The stale policy. The model recommended a discontinued product, because two-year-old conversations were never filtered by date or checked against current policy. Fix: date filters, a policy-consistency check on targets, and a regression eval on current-policy questions.

The contaminated win. A fine-tuned model scored 12 points above the base model on the team's eval, and 3 points above on freshly written items. Eval questions had come from the same logs. Fix: decontamination before training, eval sets drawn from a separate period or source, and fresh-item checks.

The over-filter. A quality classifier removed 70% of Spanish conversations as "low quality" because it was trained on English examples, and the model's Spanish got worse. Fix: per-language thresholds or classifiers, and auditing removals by slice.

The unremovable source. A data provider later withdrew permission for its content, and the team had no record of which training examples came from it, so the only option was to rebuild the whole dataset from scratch. Fix: per-example provenance from ingestion onwards, so a source can be filtered out and the model retrained on a known subset.

What to track

For each dataset version, track counts after every stage; duplicate-cluster size distribution; filter removal rates by slice; the decontamination report (flagged examples and eval items); PII detector recall on the seeded sample and the residual estimate; source and licence breakdown; the synthetic share; and results of the ablations and the memorisation test that justified the version.
myths: More fine-tuning data is always better.

Quality and diversity matter more than volume once a basic amount is reached. LIMA fine-tuned a 65B model on 1,000 carefully curated examples and its responses were judged equivalent to or better than GPT-4's in 43% of comparisons. Adding thousands of noisy or duplicated examples can make a model worse, by teaching it errors or overweighting a few patterns.
Exact deduplication is enough.

Most duplication in real data is near-duplication: the same article with different boilerplate, the same support macro with a different customer name, the same template with a changed number. Lee et al. found near-duplicates throughout standard training sets. Exact hashing misses all of these; near-duplicate detection such as MinHash finds them.
MinHash tells you exactly how similar two documents are.

MinHash estimates Jaccard similarity from a sample of hash functions, with an error that shrinks with the number of hashes: in the hand example, 8 hashes estimated 0.5 for a true similarity of 0.6, and even 128 hashes leave a standard error of about 0.04. That's fine for finding candidates at scale, and pairs near the threshold can be checked exactly.
Decontamination is only needed for public benchmarks.

Your own eval set can leak into fine-tuning data through production logs that include eval inputs, synthetic data generated from eval items, or examples copied by an engineer. Every fine-tuning dataset should be checked for overlap with every eval set used to judge the resulting model.
If data is publicly accessible, it's fine to train on.

Public is not the same as licensed. Text and code come with licences (permissive, copyleft, non-commercial) and terms of service; model outputs come with provider terms; personal data has legal protections wherever it was found. Record the source and licence of every dataset and make a deliberate decision for each.
lab:
Goal: build a MinHash near-duplicate detector with LSH banding, reproduce the hand example, and run decontamination and PII checks on a toy corpus. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. In ev11_lab.py, write shingles(text, n) returning the set of word n-grams after lower-casing and stripping punctuation, and jaccard(a, b). Check that the two body sentences give 0.6 with n = 2.
  2. Write minhash(shingle_set, k, seed). Map each shingle to an integer with hashlib.blake2b (8-byte digest), then apply k hash functions h(x) = (a·x + b) mod p with p = 261 − 1 and random a, b from random.Random(seed). Return the k minima. Estimate the two sentences' similarity with k = 8, 32, 128 and 512 and compare with 0.6.
  3. Reproduce the body's hand table exactly. Use the bigram numbering 0-9 and the 8 (a, b) pairs with p = 11, and confirm 4 matches.
  4. Build a toy corpus of about 200 support replies: 20 base templates, each with 5-15 variants (changed names, numbers, one swapped word), plus unique replies. Implement banding with b = 14, r = 8 (k = 112). Find candidate pairs, union them into clusters, and report precision and recall of the duplicate decision against your known template groups at true Jaccard ≥ 0.7.
  5. Decontamination: hold out 10 replies as an "eval set", insert 3 of them (one paraphrased) into the training corpus, and detect them with a 13-gram check and with Jaccard ≥ 0.5. Which method catches the paraphrase?
  6. PII: write regexes for emails and phone numbers and a Luhn check for card numbers. Seed 50 PII strings into the corpus and report recall.

What to look for. The MinHash estimate should converge on 0.6 as k grows, with spread around √(0.24/k). The banded detector should catch nearly all variants of long templates but miss some very short ones, where one changed word drops Jaccard below the threshold. The 13-gram check catches exact copies but not the paraphrase. Card-like numbers that fail the Luhn check are correctly ignored.
recap: Curation turns raw sources (production logs, expert-written examples, public datasets, synthetic data) into training data through cleaning, deduplication, quality filtering, mixing, decontamination, and PII and licence checks.
Exact deduplication hashes normalised text; near-duplicate detection compares sets of shingles (overlapping n-grams) by Jaccard similarity, |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|.

MinHash estimates Jaccard similarity: for a random hash function the minimum hash over A equals the minimum over B with probability J; with k hash functions the share of matching minima estimates J, with standard error √(J(1 − J)/k).
In the worked example two support sentences differing by one word have 8 shingles each, 6 shared, true Jaccard 0.6; 8 hand-computed hash functions matched on 4, estimating 0.5.

Locality-sensitive hashing groups signatures into b bands of r rows so that only likely pairs are compared; FineWeb's 14 bands of 8 make a pair at similarity 0.75 a candidate 77% of the time, at 0.8 92%, and at 0.5 only 5%.

Deduplication matters: Lee et al. found a 61-word sentence repeated over 60,000 times in C4, and deduplicated training made models emit memorised text ten times less often, while train-test overlap affected over 4% of some validation sets.

Quality filters range from heuristic rules (length, symbol ratios, language) to model-based classifiers; LIMA showed 1,000 curated examples can go a long way, and FineWeb-Edu filtered 1.3T educational tokens from FineWeb with a classifier.
Mixtures set the share of each source; small high-value sources get repeated (more epochs) and large noisy ones down-sampled, with evals per capability to tune the weights.

Decontaminate every training set against every eval set with n-gram (e.g. 13-gram) and embedding overlap; detect and mask PII and measure the detector's recall; record source, licence and processing for each dataset in a datasheet.
glossary: Band (LSH)
A group of r consecutive MinHash values; two documents become candidates if all r values in any band match.
Datasheet
Documentation for a dataset recording its motivation, sources, composition, collection process, preprocessing, licences and intended uses.
Decontamination
Removing training examples that overlap with evaluation data, so evaluations measure generalisation rather than memory.
Epoch
One full pass over a dataset during training; repeating a small source several times means several epochs over it.
Exact deduplication
Removing items whose normalised text is identical, usually by comparing hashes.
Jaccard similarity
The size of the intersection of two sets divided by the size of their union.
Locality-sensitive hashing (LSH)
A technique that hashes similar items into the same bucket with high probability, so near-duplicates can be found without comparing every pair.
MinHash

A method for estimating Jaccard similarity: for each of k hash functions, keep the minimum hash value over a set's elements; the fraction of matching minima between two sets estimates their Jaccard similarity.
Mixture weights
The proportions in which different data sources are sampled into a training set.
Near-duplicate
Two items that are nearly the same, such as the same text with different boilerplate or a few changed words.
PII (personally identifiable information)
Information that can identify a person directly or in combination, such as names, emails, phone numbers, addresses and account numbers.
Quality classifier
A model trained to score documents or examples for quality, used to filter training data.
Shingle
An overlapping sequence of n words or characters taken from a document; a document is represented as its set of shingles.
Signature (MinHash)
The vector of k minimum hash values representing one document.
Suffix array
A sorted array of all suffixes of a text, used to find repeated substrings efficiently; Lee et al. used it for exact substring deduplication.
Provenance
The record of where each dataset or example came from and what was done to it.
drill:
Diagnose and design: the fine-tune that looked too good

Your team fine-tuned a model on 300,000 support conversations. On your 1,000-item eval it scores 89% against the base model's 74%. A colleague writes 150 fresh questions in the same style, and on those the fine-tuned model scores 77% against the base model's 73%. Users report that it often ends replies with "Is there anything else I can help you with today? Have a wonderful day!" and occasionally mentions a promotion that ended last year. Explain what probably happened and how you'd rebuild the dataset.

Answer

Diagnosis. The large gap between the original eval (+15 points) and fresh questions (+4) points to contamination. The eval items, or near-copies of them, are probably in the training data. Check with a 13-gram overlap and embedding similarity between the 1,000 eval items and the training set, and see how much of the 15-point gain sits on overlapping items. The repeated sign-off means a templated closing appears in a huge share of training targets, overweighted by duplication. The expired promotion means the data wasn't filtered by date or checked against current policy.

Rebuild.

  • Clean: drop conversations older than the current policy period, or check targets against a list of current products and promotions. Drop escalated and corrected conversations.
  • Dedup: exact hashing, then substring-level removal of long repeated spans in agent replies (the sign-off), then MinHash near-duplicate collapsing on conversations (5-word shingles, about 112-128 hashes, banding tuned near a 0.8 threshold) to shrink templated macros to a few representatives.
  • Quality: keep conversations that resolved without follow-up and were rated well, scored by a classifier trained on expert labels. Audit removals by language and intent.
  • Mixture: add expert-written examples for weak intents, upsampled, and verified synthetic cases for rare ones. Tune shares on per-capability evals.
  • Decontaminate: remove every training example overlapping any eval item by 13-gram or embedding check. Rebuild the eval from a separate period, plus the 150 fresh items, and keep eval sets in a store the training pipeline can't read.
  • PII and licence: mask PII and measure detector recall, run a memorisation test, and write a datasheet.

Validate. Ablate: old dataset, rebuilt dataset, and rebuilt without decontamination, all evaluated on the clean eval and fresh items with paired comparisons. Expect a smaller but honest gain over the base model, no sign-off parroting, and no expired promotions.
qa: E
Why does deduplication matter for fine-tuning data?

Duplicates overweight a few examples, so the model memorises and over-produces them; they waste compute; and duplicates of eval items inflate scores. Lee et al. found a single 61-word sentence repeated over 60,000 times in C4, and showed that deduplicated training made models emit memorised text ten times less often with equal or better accuracy. In fine-tuning data, templated support macros and repeated boilerplate are the usual culprits.
E
What is Jaccard similarity, and how are documents turned into sets?

Jaccard similarity is |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|, the overlap of two sets relative to their union. Documents become sets by shingling: take every overlapping sequence of n words (or characters). Two sentences that differ by one word share most of their word bigrams: in the worked example 6 of 10 distinct bigrams, Jaccard 0.6. Longer documents with a small change score higher, because the change affects a smaller share of shingles.
E
What should a datasheet for a fine-tuning dataset record?

Why it was built and for what use; its sources and their licences or terms; how it was collected and by whom; its composition (sizes, languages, slices, synthetic share); all preprocessing (deduplication, filters, PII handling, decontamination) with versions and thresholds; known gaps and biases; and permitted and prohibited uses. It's what lets someone later answer 'can we use this?' and 'why does the model do that?'
M
Explain how MinHash estimates Jaccard similarity, and why it works.

Apply a random hash function to every shingle in A and in B, and keep each set's minimum. Imagine the hash ordering all shingles in A ∪ B: the smallest one is equally likely to be any element of the union, and the two minima are equal exactly when that element is in both sets, which happens with probability |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B| = J. Repeat with k independent hash functions; the fraction of equal minima estimates J with standard error √(J(1 − J)/k). Each document is then represented by a short signature of k numbers instead of its full shingle set.

Follow-up: In your hand example 8 hashes gave 0.5 for a true 0.6. Is that a bug? — No; with k = 8 the standard error is about 0.17, so 0.5 is well within noise; production systems use around 100 or more hashes.
M
How does LSH banding make near-duplicate search scale?

Comparing every pair of signatures is quadratic. Split each k-value signature into b bands of r values; hash each band; documents sharing any band's hash become candidates, and only candidates are compared. A pair with similarity s matches all r values in a band with probability s^r, so it becomes a candidate with probability 1 − (1 − s^r)^b. With FineWeb's b = 14, r = 8, that's 77% at s = 0.75, 92% at 0.8 and 5% at 0.5, an S-shaped curve with its threshold near (1/b)^(1/r) ≈ 0.72.

Follow-up: How do you move the threshold? — More rows per band raise the threshold and sharpen the curve; more bands lower it; choose b and r so the curve's steep part sits at the similarity you consider duplicate.
M
How do you build quality filters for a fine-tuning dataset drawn from support logs?

Start with rules: drop conversations that are too short or too long, not in the target language, mostly boilerplate, or where the agent's reply was later corrected or escalated. Then a model-based filter: label a few hundred examples as good or bad training targets with domain experts, and train a small classifier or use a validated LLM judge to score the rest, keeping the top share. Audit what each filter removes, by slice, because filters can silently remove whole kinds of legitimate data (short answers, a minority language).
Follow-up: What's a strong positive signal in logs? — Outcomes: conversations that resolved without follow-up contact and got good ratings are better targets than ones that merely look fluent.
M
How do you decontaminate a fine-tuning set against your eval sets?

Normalise text the same way for both, then flag any training example that shares a long n-gram with any eval item, such as 13 consecutive words as the GPT-3 paper used, plus an embedding-similarity check above a threshold to catch paraphrases. Review flagged pairs, remove contaminated training examples, and record what was removed. Re-run whenever either the training data or the eval sets change, and keep eval sets in a separate store so pipelines can't ingest them.

Follow-up: Why both n-gram and embedding checks? — N-grams catch copies and light edits cheaply; embeddings catch paraphrases and synthetic variants generated from eval items, which share meaning but few long n-grams.
M
Describe how you'd set mixture weights across data sources.

List sources with size and value: say 40k support transcripts, 2k expert-written examples, 20k synthetic examples. Decide target shares from what each teaches, e.g. 50/20/30 for a 30k-example training set, which means 15k transcripts (under one epoch), 6k expert examples (three epochs over 2k) and 9k synthetic. Small, high-quality sources are repeated; large noisy ones are down-sampled. Then tune with evals per capability: if tone improves but policy accuracy drops, shift weight. Watch for overfitting on heavily repeated small sources.

Follow-up: How many epochs over a small source is too many? — There's no universal number; watch held-out loss on that source and memorisation tests, and stop increasing repetition when held-out performance stops improving or verbatim regurgitation appears.
H
Your fine-tuned support model starts reproducing a customer's phone number in replies. What went wrong and how do you fix the pipeline?

PII made it into training data and was memorised, probably repeated: the same customer appearing in many conversations, or a template containing real details. Fix the incident first: pull the model, assess exposure, follow the incident process. Then the pipeline: PII detection combining patterns (emails, phone formats, card numbers with a Luhn check) with a named-entity model for names and addresses; replacement with consistent placeholders or realistic fakes; measuring the detector's recall on a labelled sample with seeded PII; deduplication to remove repeated records; and a memorisation test before release that prompts the model with prefixes of training records and checks for verbatim continuations.

Follow-up: The detector has 94% recall. Is that acceptable? — It means about 6% of PII instances survive; whether that's acceptable depends on volume and sensitivity, and it usually calls for layered defences such as dropping fields entirely where possible rather than relying on detection alone.
H
How do you know your curation actually helped the fine-tuned model?

Ablate: train on the raw data, on data after each curation step, and on the final set, with the same compute, and evaluate each on the same suite. Use paired comparisons per capability and per slice (ev7), plus memorisation and safety tests. This is how dataset papers like FineWeb justify each step. If ablations are too expensive at full scale, run them with a smaller model or fewer steps, accepting that some effects change with scale.

Follow-up: A filter improved the average but hurt one language slice. What then? — Inspect what it removed for that language; filters trained mostly on English often misjudge other languages, so use per-language thresholds or a different filter for that slice.
H
What licensing and provenance questions must be answered before fine-tuning on a dataset?

Where did each part come from and under what terms: our own production data (do our terms and privacy policy allow training, is there consent, are there retention limits?), public datasets (licence: permissive, copyleft, non-commercial, share-alike?), scraped content (terms of service, robots and opt-out signals), model-generated data (the provider's terms on using outputs for training), and contractor-written data (who owns it). Then: does the intended use of the model (commercial, open release) fit every licence, and can we trace and remove a source if a rights-holder objects? A datasheet records the answers, and lineage tracking makes removal possible.

Follow-up: Why does removability matter? — Because data-subject deletion requests, licence disputes or discovered contamination may require retraining without specific data, which is only practical if you know exactly which examples came from where.
H
Design a curation pipeline for fine-tuning a model on two years of customer-support conversations.

Ingest with consent and legal review; parse into conversation turns; drop non-target languages and broken records. PII: detect and replace with consistent placeholders, measure recall on a seeded sample. Exact dedup on normalised text, then near-dup with MinHash (5-word shingles, about 100-128 hashes, banding tuned to a 0.8 threshold) to collapse templated macros. Quality: rules (length, boilerplate share, escalated or corrected replies removed) plus a classifier trained on expert labels, keeping resolved, well-rated conversations. Mix with expert-written examples for weak areas and verified synthetic examples for rare intents. Decontaminate against all eval sets with 13-gram and embedding checks. Version everything with a datasheet. Validate with ablations and a memorisation test before release.
Follow-up: Which step would you never skip under time pressure? — PII handling and decontamination: one creates legal and user harm, the other makes every subsequent evaluation untrustworthy.
refs: Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better (Lee et al., 2021)

Exact substring (suffix array) and approximate (MinHash) deduplication; a 61-word sentence repeated over 60,000 times in C4; ten times less memorised output; over 4% train-test overlap in some validation sets.
On the resemblance and containment of documents (Broder, 1997)
The original MinHash idea: estimating resemblance (Jaccard similarity) of documents from minimum hash values of their shingles.
15T tokens from 96 Common Crawl snapshots with documented deduplication and filtering ablations; FineWeb-Edu's 1.3T educational tokens.
The MinHash configuration used for FineWeb: 5-gram shingles, 14 buckets of 8 hashes, applied per dump.
LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment (Zhou et al., 2023)
A 65B model fine-tuned on 1,000 curated examples, judged equivalent or better than GPT-4 in 43% of comparisons.
A standard template for documenting a dataset's motivation, composition, collection, preprocessing and uses.
Concise reference for the MinHash estimator, its variance, and banding-based locality-sensitive hashing, with links to the primary literature (including Mining of Massive Datasets, chapter 3).

t: Evals in CI and production: gates, versioning, tracing, sampling, drift alerts and the dashboard
sum: Running evaluation as a system: tiered eval suites in CI with record/replay, regression gates built from must-pass cases, paired non-inferiority and slice floors, eval-set and grader versioning, tracing with OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions, sampling production for judged and human review, drift alerts with control charts (EWMA catches a 2-point drop in about 7 days versus 17 for a 3-sigma threshold), and the one-page dashboard a team actually uses, with GitHub Copilot's evaluation practice as the case.
prereq: ae7

Prompts, models, retrieval and guardrails are bundled in a versioned release manifest; eval suites run in tiers on pull requests, before release and continuously; rollouts go shadow, canary, ramp with rollback.
ae3
Quality degrades silently through drift and provider changes; monitoring layers run from system health to business outcomes; drift statistics have a sample-size noise floor.
ev4
LLM judges are validated against human labels, pinned and versioned, and corrected for known error rates; judges drift too.
ev7
Compare versions with paired differences and intervals; set gates above A/A noise; correct for many slices; prefer non-inferiority to 'not significantly worse'.
ev8
Online tests with primary and guardrail metrics are the final verdict for major changes; implicit signals are biased and must be validated.
why:
A team has done everything the earlier topics in this track recommend, once. They built a golden set from real traffic (ev2), validated an LLM judge against expert labels (ev4), computed paired comparisons with intervals (ev7) and ran an A/B test for their last model change (ev8). Six months later the practice has quietly decayed. The eval script lives on one engineer's laptop and runs when someone remembers. A prompt change shipped on a Friday with "looked fine on a few examples". The judge prompt was edited in March, so scores before and after aren't comparable, and nobody wrote that down. Production logs exist, but as unstructured text in a bucket that's deleted after 14 days, and nobody looks at them. There is a dashboard with 41 charts. When quality drops after the provider quietly updates the model, the first signal is a customer escalation two weeks later.

This is the normal fate of evaluation that isn't built into the engineering system. The methods in this track only protect a product if they run automatically, on every change and continuously in production. Their results must be stored so they can be compared, failures must reach a person who acts on them, and the loop must close back into the eval suite. ae7 covered the release side of LLMOps: manifests, continuous-integration (CI) tiers, canaries and rollback. ae3 covered production monitoring and drift. This lesson builds the evaluation system that connects them, the senior engineer's answer to "how do you know it still works next week?"

It covers seven things. Running eval suites in CI within a time and cost budget, including record/replay. Designing regression gates that catch what matters without flapping, worked through a gate's actual logic. Versioning eval sets and graders so results stay comparable. Tracing production requests in a standard, privacy-safe structure. Sampling production for judged and human review, with the sample sizes. Alerting on quality drift with control charts, worked by simulation to show why the obvious daily threshold is slow. And the one-page eval dashboard a team actually reads. The case is GitHub's description of how the Copilot team evaluates models: thousands of tests in CI, an audited judge, and canary rollouts to employees.
primer:
A factory that makes a precision part doesn't rely on an inspector glancing at a few parts at the end of the week. It has a quality system. Incoming material is checked before it enters the line, which is the CI gate. Every batch carries a record of which machine, which settings and which material lot produced it, the trace and the version keys. Inspectors pull parts from the line at regular intervals, at random and whenever a sensor flags something, which is production sampling. Measurements go on control charts pinned to the wall, with limits that tell the shift supervisor when the process has drifted, not just when a single part is bad. That is drift alerting. One board shows the handful of numbers that say whether the line is healthy, the dashboard. And every defect that reaches a customer is traced back to its cause, and a new check is added so it can't recur. That last step is the loop.

The analogy carries further than it might seem. Control charts were invented in manufacturing in the 1920s for exactly the problem LLM teams face: telling a real shift in a process from normal variation, using small samples taken over time. Where the analogy breaks is the parts. An LLM system's "process" includes components the team doesn't control, such as the provider's model, user behaviour and the documents in the index. So the quality system must watch inputs and dependencies, not just outputs.

The closed evaluation loop

Read the loop from left to right along the top. A change passes through CI eval tiers: a fast smoke suite on every pull request, a full suite before merge or release, and exhaustive runs nightly. A regression gate decides whether it may proceed. It goes through a canary and is released. Then along the bottom, from right to left. Production requests are traced, traces are sampled, and the sample is graded with the same graders as the offline suite: assertions, a validated judge and a human subset. Grades feed control charts that alert on drift and a dashboard. Flagged items are triaged, and confirmed failures become new eval cases that gate the next change. Underneath it all, every result is stored with its version keys, so any number can be reproduced and compared with the right baseline.

Notice that the same graders appear on both paths. The policy judge that gates a release in CI is the judge that grades the production sample, and the assertions that block a pull request are the assertions that run on live responses. That symmetry is deliberate: it means an offline score and a production score measure the same thing, so a gap between them points at a real difference in inputs or behaviour rather than at two inconsistent rulers.

None of the pieces is new to this track. What this lesson adds is the engineering that makes them run every day without heroics: budgets, gate logic, storage, sampling arithmetic, alert design and ownership.
body:
1. Eval suites in CI: tiers, budgets and record/replay

ae7 introduced eval tiers. The engineering challenge is making them fast and cheap enough that nobody is tempted to skip them. A useful split, with typical budgets:

TierWhenContentsBudget
SmokeEvery pull request200-500 cases: assertions, must-pass cases, recorded responses where valid< 5-10 min, near-zero model cost
FullBefore merge of prompt/model/retrieval changes; release candidatesFull golden set, 3 samples/item, live model calls, validated judges, slices, safety suite30-60 min, tens of dollars
Nightly / scheduledDaily on main and on production configEverything, plus red-team runs, long-tail suites, probe sets against productionHours, budgeted monthly

Two techniques keep the smoke tier fast. Record/replay: when a change can't affect what goes into the model, such as a refactor of response formatting or a change to logging, replay model responses recorded from the last live run. Tests then run in seconds, cost nothing and are deterministic. When a change can affect the model's input (the prompt template, retrieved context, tool schemas, model parameters), replayed responses are invalid, and the affected suites must run live. Deciding which is which is the second technique, change-based suite selection. Map files and configuration to the suites they can affect. A change to the refund prompt triggers the refund feature's live suite. A change to the chunker triggers retrieval metrics and the RAG suite. A change to shared infrastructure triggers everything.

Cost controls matter for the full tier. Cache judge verdicts keyed by a hash of (judge version, rubric version, input, output), so unchanged outputs aren't re-judged. Run calls in parallel within provider rate limits. Track eval cost and runtime as metrics in their own right. An eval suite whose cost doubles every quarter will eventually be cut, usually at the worst moment.

2. Regression gates that catch what matters

A regression gate is code that reads eval results and returns pass or fail with reasons. ae7 worked a paired comparison that blocked a release because one slice collapsed. Here is the full structure of a gate, as a team would implement it:

def gate(candidate, baseline, cfg):
    reasons = []
    # 1. Must-pass cases: every trial must pass
    for case in cfg.must_pass:
        if not all(candidate.trials[case]):
            reasons.append(f"must-pass failed: {case}")
    # 2. Aggregate non-inferiority on paired per-item scores
    d = [candidate.score[i] - baseline.score[i] for i in cfg.items]
    lo, hi = paired_ci(d)                          # ev7: paired SE or bootstrap
    if lo < -cfg.margin:                           # e.g. margin = 0.015
        reasons.append(f"aggregate: lower bound {lo:+.3f} below -{cfg.margin}")
    # 3. Slice floors with Holm correction across gate slices
    for s, p_value, score in holm_adjusted(candidate, baseline, cfg.gate_slices):
        if score < cfg.floor[s] and p_value < 0.05:
            reasons.append(f"slice {s}: {score:.1%} below floor {cfg.floor[s]:.0%}")
    # 4. Guardrails
    if candidate.schema_valid_rate < 0.995: reasons.append("schema validity")
    if candidate.p95_latency_ms > baseline.p95_latency_ms + 300: reasons.append("latency")
    if candidate.cost_per_req > 1.10 * baseline.cost_per_req: reasons.append("cost")
    return (len(reasons) == 0, reasons)

Each component catches a different kind of regression. Must-pass cases are the non-negotiables: legal requirements, safety behaviours, money limits. They are run several times and must pass every time, because pass^k is what matters for them (ev1). The aggregate non-inferiority check uses a paired comparison with a margin (ev7). It asks "is the candidate not worse than baseline by more than 1.5 points, with 95% confidence?", rather than "is it not significantly worse?", which a noisy suite always passes. Slice floors catch the collapse of one slice that an average hides, with a correction across the gate slices so five slices don't create a 23% chance of a false block. Guardrails catch improvements bought with latency, cost or broken formatting.

Worked: a candidate prompt for the support assistant, run against baseline on the full tier.

CheckResultThresholdVerdict
Must-pass (60 cases × 3 trials)60/60 all trialsallpass
Aggregate policy correctness (800 items, paired)+0.9 pts, 95% CI −0.6 to +2.4lower bound ≥ −1.5pass
Slice: refund disputes (n = 120)88.3% vs floor 90%, Holm-adjusted p = 0.21below floor and significantpass, flagged
Slice: legal requests (n = 80)97.5%floor 95%pass
Schema validity99.8%≥ 99.5%pass
p95 latency+420 ms≤ +300 msfail
Cost per request+6%≤ +10%pass

The gate fails on latency. The new prompt is longer and pushes the model to write more. Quality is fine, so the fix is to trim the prompt or cap output length, not to abandon the change. The refund-disputes slice is below its floor but not significantly, given its noise, so the gate passes it and flags it for the next run. That is the right behaviour for a 120-item slice whose interval is about ±6 points.

Flakiness is the gate's main enemy. Measure the suite's A/A noise by running the same configuration ten times every month or so, and set margins above it (ev7). Replay where valid. Quarantine cases that flip without cause and fix them, rather than re-running the gate until it goes green. Make overrides possible but costly: a named approver and a written reason, recorded with the release. A gate that is overridden every week is telling you its thresholds or its cases are wrong.

How do you know the gate works? Test it. Seed known-bad candidates, such as a prompt with the refund-limit sentence deleted, a cheaper model known to be worse, or a retrieval config with half the index missing, and check that the gate blocks each. This is mutation testing for the eval system. It measures the gate's sensitivity, which is otherwise only discovered when a real regression gets through.

3. Versioning: eval sets, graders and results

An eval result is a function of four things: the system (the release manifest from ae7), the eval set, the grader (judge model, judge prompt, rubric, parsing code) and the harness (sampling settings, number of trials, aggregation). Change any one and the number changes. So every stored result is keyed by all four:

result_key = (manifest="support-2026.10.03-r2",
              eval_set="support-golden@v7 (sha256:9c1e…)",
              grader="policy-judge@v4 (model=judge-2026-08, rubric=r12)",
              harness="harness@1.8 (trials=3, temp=0.7)")

The rules follow. Eval sets are immutable once versioned. Changing a case creates a new version, identified by a content hash so silent edits are impossible. Each version has a changelog: cases added from production failures, cases retired, expected answers updated after a policy change. Graders are versioned the same way, and a new grader version is validated against human labels before use (ev4). Comparisons are only made between results that differ in exactly one key, usually the manifest. When the eval set or grader changes, re-run the baseline on the new version to create a bridge, so trend lines can continue. Some teams keep a small anchor set and anchor grader that never change, purely for long-run trends (ev2).

Store results at the item level, not just aggregates: per case, per trial, every grader's verdict and reasoning, with the trace of the system's run. Item-level storage is what makes paired comparisons, slice breakdowns and "show me what changed" diffs possible. Frameworks such as Inspect write structured logs with every sample, score and transcript for this reason.

4. Tracing production requests

Production evaluation starts with data, and the right shape for that data is a trace: one record per request, made of nested spans, one per step, each timed and annotated. For a RAG assistant with tools:

Useful attributes per span: for model calls, the model identifier as returned by the API, the prompt template version, sampling parameters, input and output token counts, latency, finish reason. For retrieval, the query, the returned document IDs and scores, and the index version. For tool calls, the name, arguments (redacted where sensitive), result status and latency. At the trace level, the release manifest ID, a pseudonymous user or session ID, the channel, and links to feedback events that arrive later. Feedback includes thumbs, edits and escalations (ev8).

Use a standard schema rather than inventing one. The OpenTelemetry project maintains semantic conventions for generative AI, standard names for these attributes and spans, now kept in a dedicated repository. Examples are gen_ai.operation.name, gen_ai.request.model and gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, with conventions for agents, tool execution and evaluation as well. Standard names let tracing tools, dashboards and eval pipelines interoperate. The conventions are still evolving, so pin the version you implement.

Two constraints shape what you store. Privacy: redact personal data at write time, not later, and store raw content only where policy allows (ae5). Retention: keep full content for a short window for debugging, keep structured metadata longer for trends, and copy sampled, consented and scrubbed traces into the eval store when they become cases. ae7 called this trade-off debuggability versus data retention. The design decision is made once, deliberately, rather than discovered during an incident.

Traces also enable replay. A production trace's inputs (message, retrieved documents, tool results) can be fed to a candidate system offline, to see how it would have answered the same request. That turns production traffic into a ready-made eval set. Traces that led to failures become regression cases, and random traces become fresh representative samples.

5. Sampling production for review

You can't have humans read every conversation, and you may not want to pay a judge for every one. Production sampling has two different jobs, and they need different samples.

Job 1: an unbiased estimate of quality. This needs a random sample, ideally stratified by slice (ev2), graded by a validated judge. The sample size comes from the precision you need. For a weekly estimate within ±3 points at around 85% quality: n = 1.96² × 0.85 × 0.15 / 0.03² ≈ 545 judged conversations a week. For ±3 points in each of five slices, about 545 per slice. A human-labelled subset of 100-150 a week measures the judge's ongoing agreement and specificity (ev4). If the judge's error rates are known, the estimate can be corrected for them (the Rogan-Gladen correction from ev4).

Job 2: finding failures fast. This needs a targeted sample, items selected because a signal suggests trouble. Candidates include thumbs-down and escalations, regenerations, low judge confidence (probability of PASS near 0.5), guardrail flags, long or looping agent traces, conversations in new intent clusters (ae3), and outputs that changed most between releases. Targeted samples are where reviewers find new failure modes several times faster than random reading. They are deliberately unrepresentative, so they are never mixed into the quality estimate unless reweighted.

Worked: 50,000 conversations a week. Draw a 1.2% random sample, 600 conversations stratified across five intents, and grade them with the validated judge. That gives about ±2.9 points on the weekly headline. Send 120 of those to human reviewers for judge calibration. Draw 200 targeted conversations from negative signals for human triage. Total human load is about 320 reviews a week, roughly 8-11 hours at 30-40 an hour, which fits within one person's part-time role. Judge cost for 600 conversations with three criteria is a few dollars at the prices assumed in ev1. Running the judge on 100% of traffic would also be affordable at this volume. That is a reasonable choice, removing sampling error, but the human subset remains essential.

6. Alerting on quality drift with control charts

With a daily judged sample, you have a time series of quality. When should it alert? The obvious design is a threshold: alert if today's pass rate falls more than three standard errors below normal. That is a Shewhart chart, the basic control chart. It is good at catching big, sudden drops and poor at catching small, persistent ones, which are exactly what silent provider updates and slow input drift produce.

Worked: 500 judged conversations a day, normal pass rate 85%. The daily standard error is √(0.85 × 0.15 / 500) = 0.016, or 1.6 points. A 3-sigma limit sits 4.8 points below the mean, at 80.2%. On a normal day the chance of a false alarm is about 0.13%, roughly one every couple of years of daily checks. Now suppose quality drops by 2 points, to 83%. A single day's pass rate falls below 80.2% only occasionally, because the drop is small relative to the daily noise.

An EWMA chart (exponentially weighted moving average) accumulates evidence. Each day it updates zt = λxt + (1 − λ)zt−1, where xt is today's pass rate and λ, often 0.2, sets how quickly old days are forgotten. The EWMA is much less noisy than a single day. Its long-run standard deviation is σ√(λ/(2 − λ)) = 1.6 × √(0.2/1.8) = 1.6 × 0.333 ≈ 0.53 points. So its 3-sigma limit sits only 1.6 points below the mean, at 83.4%. A persistent 2-point drop pulls the EWMA steadily towards 83%, and it crosses the limit within days.

A simulation makes the comparison concrete. 300 runs, 500 judged items a day, 10 normal days at 85%, then a persistent drop:

Drop3-sigma daily threshold: days to alarm (mean / median / 90th pct)EWMA λ = 0.2, 3-sigma limit
85% → 83% (2 points)17.3 / 12 / 357.0 / 6 / 11
85% → 82% (3 points)6.3 / 4.5 / 144.0 / 4 / 6
85% → 80% (5 points)1.8 / 1 / 32.3 / 2 / 3

The pattern is the one statistical process control has taught since the 1920s. Single-observation limits are best for large shifts. Accumulating charts, EWMA and its cousin CUSUM (cumulative sum, which adds up deviations from target and alarms when the sum crosses a threshold), are best for small, persistent ones. Run both: a Shewhart limit for outages and an EWMA or CUSUM for drift. The false-alarm rates are comparable. In the simulation, the EWMA chart with no real change ran for several hundred days on average before a false alarm, similar to the 3-sigma threshold's roughly 740-day average. The average run length (ARL) is the standard way to compare charts: long when nothing has changed, short after a real shift.

Quality is not the only thing to chart. Leading indicators often move first: input drift (the intent mix, language mix, input length, ae3), grader health (the judge's verdicts on a fixed set of stored outputs with known verdicts, which should never change, so any change is judge drift), the serving model identifier returned by the API (a change means the provider changed something), guardrail and refusal rates, implicit feedback rates (ev8), latency and cost. Each alert needs an owner and a runbook: what to check first, how to tell system drift from judge drift from input drift, and when to roll back. Too many alerts without owners produce alert fatigue, and then the important one is ignored.

7. The dashboard a team actually uses

Most eval dashboards fail by showing too much. The one teams use answers the questions they actually ask, in roughly this order, on one page:

  1. Is quality where it should be? Headline quality per product surface from the random production sample, with intervals, a trend line and alert state.
  2. Did the last change hurt anything? Candidate against current release from the full CI tier: aggregate with interval, gate slices against floors, guardrails, and gate verdict.
  3. Can we trust the graders? Judge-human agreement, kappa and specificity on the latest calibration sample, and the drift check on the fixed set (ev4).
  4. What is failing? Top failure categories from this week's triage, with counts and the share that now have eval cases.
  5. What does it cost? Cost and latency per request, and eval spend.
  6. Where are the examples? Every number links to example traces, an owner and a runbook.

What's left off matters as much: raw counts without intervals, metrics that no one owns or acts on, and diagnostic charts that only matter during an investigation, which belong in drill-down views. A good test of any chart is to ask what decision someone would make if it moved. If nobody can say, remove it.

8. Closing the loop: triage, ownership and the weekly review

The loop closes through people. Flagged and sampled failures go into a triage queue. A reviewer reads each one, assigns a cause from a maintained failure taxonomy (retrieval miss, stale document, policy misread, tool error, tone, injection attempt…) and a severity (ev9), and decides the action: a bug, a prompt change, a data fix, or "acceptable". Every confirmed failure becomes an eval case with provenance, generalised into a few variants so the fix addresses the cause rather than one phrasing, and added to a regression or targeted suite (ev2). Never add it to the representative set.

A short weekly quality review keeps the system alive. Look at the dashboard, discuss alerts and their causes, review the top failure categories, check the coverage metric (the share of failure categories with at least one eval case), and assign owners. It is the evaluation equivalent of an operations review, and teams that skip it find their dashboards drifting into wallpaper. Clear ownership underpins it. Product owners own the rubrics and cases, engineers own harness, gates and alerts, and someone owns the weekly review (ev1).
deep:
Evaluating the evaluation system

The eval system itself can fail silently: gates that never block, judges that drift, alerts that never fire. Test it like any system. Gate sensitivity: seed known-bad candidates and confirm they're blocked, and seed known-equivalent ones (an A/A) and confirm they pass. Alert sensitivity: inject a synthetic drop into a replayed quality series, or temporarily route a small share of traffic to a deliberately degraded variant in a safe slice, and measure time to alert. Coverage: track the share of production failure categories covered by eval cases, and how many production incidents were caught by an eval or alert before a user reported them. That last ratio is the single best measure of whether the evaluation system works.

Determinism and replay in practice

Record/replay needs care. Recorded responses are valid only while the model's inputs are identical, so the replay key must include everything that reaches the model: the rendered prompt, retrieved context, tool results and parameters, hashed. A mismatch must fall back to a live call, never silently reuse a stale response. Agent traces are harder, because each step depends on earlier ones. Replaying a trajectory step by step works only if every tool result is also recorded, and any divergence ends the replay. Teams often keep a replay mode for fast CI and treat live runs as the source of truth for gates.

Infrastructure changes deserve evals too

ae7's case, Anthropic's 2025 postmortem, showed quality bugs coming from serving infrastructure rather than models or prompts: routing errors, a compiler issue, a sampling bug. Such changes don't touch prompts, so naive suite selection skips them. The defence is to treat infrastructure changes (serving stack, tokeniser, quantisation, batching, hardware) as triggers for the full live suite, to run numerical-equivalence checks on fixed inputs where possible, and to keep continuous probe evals on production so a bug that slips through is visible within days.

Cost management at scale

Eval cost grows with features, suites, trials and judge criteria. Levers include caching judge verdicts, replay for non-model changes, distilling a large judge into a cheaper fine-tuned one validated against the original and humans (ev4), sampling rather than grading everything in nightly suites, retiring stale cases to slower tiers, and budgeting eval spend per team with visibility on the dashboard. The goal isn't minimal spend. It is spend proportional to the cost of regressions the evals prevent.

Multi-tenant and per-customer evaluation

Enterprise products often serve customers with different documents, policies and expectations. A global quality number can hide one large customer's collapse. Per-tenant golden sets for the largest customers, per-tenant slices in production sampling, and per-tenant floors in gates catch this. Privacy constraints often mean per-tenant data can't leave that tenant's boundary, so the harness must run where the data lives.

When evals and incidents disagree

Sometimes users report problems that every eval and alert says aren't happening. Treat this as an eval failure until proven otherwise. The sample may not cover the affected slice, the judge may be blind to that failure, or the issue may be in a channel or locale the traces don't capture. Pull the reported cases, see why the evaluation system missed them, and fix that, as well as the product bug. Each such miss should make the evaluation system strictly better.

Evaluating agents in the loop

Agents stretch every part of this system. Traces are long and branching, so spans must capture each step's tool call, arguments and result, and sampling must consider whole trajectories. Graders check outcomes in sandboxed environments (ev1), which CI must be able to create and reset quickly. Costs per eval run are higher, so tiers matter more. And drift can appear as longer trajectories, more tool errors or more retries before quality visibly drops, so steps per task and tool-error rates belong on the control charts alongside success rate. The next track, on agentic systems, builds on this foundation.

Proportionality

Not every feature needs every piece of this lesson. A low-traffic internal tool may need tracing, a 50-case CI suite and a monthly look at sampled traces. A customer-facing assistant handling money needs all of it. The senior skill is matching the evaluation system's weight to the stakes and the rate of change, and growing it as the product grows, rather than building a platform no one uses or shipping a product no one can measure.
prod:
The public case: how GitHub evaluates models for Copilot (GitHub Blog, January 2025)

GitHub's engineering post "How we evaluate AI models and LLMs for GitHub Copilot" describes an evaluation system with the shape this lesson builds. The team runs more than 4,000 offline tests, most of them as part of an automated CI pipeline, before any change reaches production. For code changes, they keep around 100 containerised repositories whose CI tests pass. They deliberately modify the code so tests fail, then measure whether a candidate model can modify the codebase to make the tests pass again. That is a functional-correctness eval (ev3) built from real repositories, with outcomes graded by execution. For completions they track the percentage of unit tests passed, similarity to the original known-good code and token usage. For chat, question-answering accuracy and token efficiency. For both, latency and acceptance rates.

For chat, where responses are open-ended, they use an LLM judge, "a model with known good performance", and they routinely audit its outputs to make sure it stays aligned with human reviewers and consistent across requests. That is ev4's validated, monitored judge. Models are also tested for toxic content, prompt-injection resistance and relevance filtering for non-code queries (ev9). And before production, major changes go through live internal evaluations, where some GitHub employees are switched to the new model, a canary on internal users (ev8, ae7).

What makes the post useful as a case is the integration: thousands of automated tests in CI, outcome-graded tasks built from real code, an audited judge for the open-ended parts, safety suites, internal canaries, and online metrics such as acceptance rate. No single piece is exotic. Together they are an evaluation system that runs on every change, which is the difference between knowing a product works and hoping it does.

Failure modes in practice

The overridden gate. A gate blocked three releases in a month on a flaky slice, so the team added a "skip evals" label. Within a quarter it was used on a third of releases, including one that shipped a regression. Fix: measure A/A noise and fix the thresholds, quarantine flaky cases, and make overrides require a named approver and a written reason that appears in the release record.

The incomparable trend. The judge prompt was edited and the quality chart jumped 5 points. For two months nobody knew whether quality had changed. Fix: version graders, re-score a bridge set with old and new graders, and annotate the chart.

Alert fatigue. Thirty alerts across input drift, latency, cost and quality fired weekly with no owners. When a real quality drop came, its alert was ignored with the rest. Fix: fewer alerts, each with an owner and runbook, control charts tuned to known false-alarm rates, and a weekly review of alert outcomes.

Traces that can't be used. Prompts and outputs were logged as free text with personal data, so legal blocked any use of them for evaluation. Fix: structured spans, redaction at write time, and a documented retention and reuse policy agreed before launch.

A checklist for an evaluation system

Tiered CI suites with budgets and record/replay. Gates with must-pass cases, paired non-inferiority, slice floors and guardrails, tested with seeded regressions. Results keyed by manifest, eval-set, grader and harness versions, stored per item. Structured, redacted traces with standard attributes. Random and targeted production sampling with a human calibration subset. Control-chart alerts on quality, graders, inputs and dependencies, each with an owner. A one-page dashboard. A triage process that turns failures into eval cases, and a weekly quality review.
myths: Running the eval suite in CI means the product is protected.

Only if the gate is designed to catch the regressions that matter and nobody routinely overrides it. A gate on the overall average misses a collapsed slice; a gate below the suite's noise flaps until engineers learn to re-run it; a gate nobody owns gets disabled. Gates need must-pass cases, slice floors, thresholds set from A/A noise, and an owner.
Offline evals and production monitoring are separate jobs.

They're one loop. Production traces are sampled and graded with the same graders as the offline suite, production failures become offline cases, and offline results are checked against production outcomes. Teams that run them separately end up with an offline suite that no longer represents traffic and monitoring that can't explain what it sees.
A daily quality threshold alert is enough to catch drift.

A single-day threshold set wide enough to avoid false alarms misses small, persistent drops: in the worked simulation a 2-point fall from 85% took a 3-sigma daily threshold 17 days on average to flag, versus 7 for an EWMA chart with a similar false-alarm rate. Use control charts that accumulate evidence, and alert on graders and inputs as well as quality.
Log everything and figure it out later.

Unstructured logs of prompts and outputs are hard to query, expensive, and a privacy liability. Structured traces, a span per step with standard attributes (model, prompt version, tokens, retrieved document IDs, tool calls) and redaction at write time, are what make sampling, debugging and replay possible within retention limits.
The best eval dashboard shows every metric.

A dashboard with forty charts is read by no one. The one teams use answers a few questions at a glance: is quality where it should be, with intervals and trend? Did the last release change anything, and where? Are the graders still trustworthy? What are the top failure categories this week? Every chart has an owner and an action.
lab:
Goal: build a tiny eval harness with a stub model and a regression gate, then an EWMA drift detector on simulated production quality. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. In ev12_lab.py, write a stub model(version, case, rng) returning pass or fail with per-slice probabilities. For example, baseline "r2" passes refunds 0.92, legal 0.97, general 0.85. Candidate "r3" passes 0.89, 0.98, 0.88, and adds latency. Include 10 must-pass cases that r2 always passes and r3 fails with probability 0.05.
  2. Build 800 cases across slices, run each version with 3 trials (seeded), and store results keyed by (version, eval_set_version, grader_version, harness_version) in a dict.
  3. Implement gate(candidate, baseline) as in the body: must-pass (all trials), paired non-inferiority with a bootstrap CI and margin 0.015, slice floors with a Holm correction, and a latency guardrail. Print the verdict and reasons.
  4. Run an A/A comparison (r2 against r2 with different seeds) ten times and print how often the gate fails. Then seed a known-bad candidate (refunds at 0.80) and confirm it is blocked.
  5. Drift: simulate 60 days of production with 500 judged items a day at 85%, dropping to 83% from day 31. Plot as text, or print, the daily rate and an EWMA with λ = 0.2. Report the first day each of the daily 3-sigma rule and the EWMA rule alarms. Repeat over 200 seeds and print the mean delay of each.

What to look for. The gate should catch the must-pass failure in most r3 runs (with 10 cases × 3 trials at 5% failure each, P(all pass) = 0.9530 ≈ 21%), so about 79% of r3 runs are blocked on must-pass alone. That shows why must-pass behaviour needs pass^k thinking. The A/A gate should rarely fail. If it fails often, the margin is below the noise. In the drift simulation the EWMA should alarm about a week after the drop on average, and the daily threshold much later and more erratically, matching the body's table.
recap: Evaluation in a mature team is a closed loop: changes pass CI eval gates, releases go through canaries, production is traced, sampled and graded, quality is tracked with alerts, and confirmed failures become new eval cases.

CI runs eval suites in tiers sized to their budget: a fast smoke suite with recorded model responses on every pull request, the full suite with live calls and judges before merge or release, and exhaustive or probe runs nightly.

A regression gate combines must-pass cases, a paired non-inferiority test on the aggregate, slice floors, and guardrails (format validity, latency, cost), with thresholds set above A/A noise and Holm correction across gate slices.
Every eval result is keyed by the system manifest, eval-set version, grader version and harness version, so results are reproducible and only like-for-like comparisons are made.

Tracing records one span per step (request, retrieval, model call, tool call) with standard attributes such as those in the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions (gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens), redacted at write time and linked to feedback.

Production sampling has two purposes: a random, stratified sample graded by a validated judge (about 545 judged items a week give ±3 points at 85%) for an unbiased quality estimate, and targeted samples (negative signals, low judge confidence, new clusters) for finding failures.

Drift alerts use control charts: with 500 judged items a day at 85%, a 3-sigma daily threshold sits 4.8 points below the mean, while an EWMA chart (λ = 0.2) detects a 2-point drop in about 7 days on average against 17 for the threshold.

The dashboard a team uses fits on one page: headline quality per surface with intervals and trend, release comparison by slice, grader health, top failure categories from triage, cost and latency, each linking to traces and each with an owner.

GitHub's Copilot team describes running more than 4,000 offline tests, mostly in CI, around 100 containerised repositories broken and then fixed by the model, an audited LLM judge for chat, and internal canary rollouts to employees before production.
glossary: A/A noise
The variation in an eval result between two runs of the same system, used to set gate thresholds.
Control chart
A time-series chart with limits computed from the process's normal variation, used to detect when a metric has shifted.
CUSUM
Cumulative sum control chart: accumulates deviations from a target and alarms when the sum crosses a threshold, sensitive to small persistent shifts.
EWMA chart
Exponentially weighted moving average chart: tracks a weighted average that gives recent days more weight, with limits that make it sensitive to small shifts.
Eval-set version
An immutable, identified snapshot of an evaluation dataset, so results computed on it can be reproduced and compared.
Must-pass case
An eval case that must pass for a release to proceed, regardless of aggregate scores.
Record/replay
Saving model responses from a live run and replaying them in later test runs, so tests are fast, cheap and deterministic when the model call isn't what changed.
Regression gate
An automated check in CI or release that blocks a change if evaluation results fall below defined criteria.
Slice floor
A minimum acceptable score for a specific slice, enforced separately from the aggregate.
Span
One timed operation within a trace, such as a retrieval, a model call or a tool call, with attributes describing it.
Stratified sampling (production)
Sampling production traffic separately within slices (intents, languages, customer tiers) to guarantee coverage, then reweighting for overall estimates.
Targeted sampling
Selecting production items for review because a signal suggests they may be failures, to find problems quickly; not representative.
Trace
The record of one request through the system, made of nested spans.
Triage
Reviewing flagged items or failures, classifying them by cause and severity, and deciding what to do about each.
Shewhart chart
The basic control chart that alarms when a single observation falls outside limits, typically three standard deviations from the mean.
Average run length (ARL)
The average number of periods before a control chart alarms; long when nothing has changed (few false alarms), short after a real shift (fast detection).
drill:
Design: evaluation operations for a new AI feature

You are the senior engineer on a new "AI answers" feature in a project-management product. It answers questions about a customer's own projects using retrieval over their tasks, documents and comments, with a few read-only tools. It launches to 10% of customers next month, about 30,000 questions a week, growing tenfold by year end. The team has an offline golden set of 400 questions, a validated judge for correctness and faithfulness, and nothing else. Design the evaluation system for launch and for the following six months.

Answer

Before launch (weeks 1-3). Instrument tracing with OpenTelemetry GenAI attribute names: request, retrieval (doc IDs, index version), model calls (model ID returned, prompt version, tokens, latency), tool calls, final answer, guardrail results, and linked feedback. Redact at write time, keep full content 14 days, keep metadata 13 months, and agree a reuse policy with legal. Build the harness. Version the 400-question set (v1) and the judge (v1). Store item-level results keyed by manifest, eval-set, grader and harness versions. Add CI tiers: a smoke suite (assertions plus 100 must-pass and representative cases, replayed for non-model changes) on every pull request, and the full suite (400 × 3 trials, live, judged) on prompt, model, retrieval and infrastructure changes. Add a gate: must-pass for tenant isolation (no cross-customer retrieval, which is an always-on assertion) and read-only tool use; paired non-inferiority on correctness and faithfulness with a 2-point margin set from A/A noise; floors on three gate slices; and latency and cost guardrails. Test the gate with seeded bad candidates.

Launch (10%). Sample about 600 questions a week at random, stratified by question type, and judge them for an estimate within roughly ±3 points. Send 120 a week to human reviewers to keep the judge calibrated (track kappa and specificity). Send 150 targeted questions a week from thumbs-down, low judge confidence and new clusters to human triage. Run control charts: daily judged quality with Shewhart and EWMA rules, a judge drift check on a fixed set, the returned model ID, input-cluster mix, refusal and guardrail rates. Each alert has an owner and runbook.

Months 2-6. Grow the golden set from triaged failures into regression and targeted suites, keeping the representative set refreshed monthly from random production samples. Add per-tenant slices for the largest customers. Raise sample sizes for per-slice precision as traffic grows, or judge 100% of traffic if cost allows. Add red-team and injection suites, especially for content in comments, which users other than the asker can write (ev9). Run online tests for major changes (ev8). Hold a one-page dashboard and a weekly quality review. Track coverage of failure categories by eval cases, and the share of incidents caught by evals or alerts before users reported them, as the measure of whether the system works.
qa: E
What does a regression gate for an LLM feature check?

That a candidate change doesn't make things worse in ways that matter: all must-pass cases pass; the aggregate quality metric is non-inferior to the current release by a set margin, using a paired comparison on the same items; each gate slice stays above its floor; and guardrails such as format validity, safety checks, latency and cost per request hold. Thresholds come from measured A/A noise so the gate doesn't flap.
E
What should a trace for an LLM request contain?

A span per step: the incoming request, retrieval (query, document IDs, scores), each model call (model and version, prompt template version, parameters, input and output token counts, latency, finish reason), each tool call (name, arguments, result status), and the final response. Plus the release manifest ID, user or session IDs as pseudonyms, and links to any feedback. Personal data is redacted at write time and retention follows policy.
E
Why version eval sets and graders?

Because a result is only meaningful relative to what it was measured on and how. If the eval set or the judge prompt changes between two runs, a difference in scores could come from the change in the instrument rather than the system. Keying every result by system manifest, eval-set version, grader version and harness version makes results reproducible and stops apples-to-oranges comparisons.
M
How do you keep an eval suite fast and cheap enough to run on every pull request?

Tier it. On every pull request run a smoke suite of a few hundred cases with assertions and, where the model call isn't what changed, recorded responses replayed deterministically, so a code refactor doesn't need live model calls. Select suites by change type: a prompt change triggers that feature's live suite; a retrieval change triggers retrieval metrics. Run the full live suite with judges before merge or release, cache judge results keyed by input hashes, and run exhaustive suites nightly. Track eval cost and runtime as metrics.

Follow-up: When is replay dangerous? — When the change can affect the model's input (prompt, retrieved context, tool schemas); then replayed outputs no longer correspond to what the model would produce, so those changes must run live.
M
How many production items should you grade each week, and how do you choose them?

Two samples with different jobs. For an unbiased quality estimate, a random sample stratified by slice and graded by a validated judge; for ±3 points at 85% you need about 545 items a week (1.96² × 0.85 × 0.15 / 0.03²), more for per-slice precision. A human-labelled subset of 100-150 measures judge agreement. Separately, targeted samples (thumbs-down, low judge confidence, guardrail flags, new intent clusters) for finding failures quickly; these aren't used for the quality estimate unless reweighted.

Follow-up: Why not just grade everything with the judge? — You can if cost allows, which removes sampling error, but you still need the human subset to know whether the judge is right, and targeted human review to understand failures.
M
How would you alert on quality drift in production?

Grade a daily sample with a validated judge and track the pass rate on a control chart. A simple 3-sigma daily threshold only catches large drops; an EWMA or CUSUM chart accumulates evidence and catches small persistent shifts faster with a similar false-alarm rate. Alert also on leading signals: input drift (new clusters, language mix), grader health (judge verdicts on a fixed reference set), guardrail rates and implicit feedback. Route alerts to an owner with a runbook, and investigate before rolling back.
Follow-up: How do you tell judge drift from system drift? — Re-run the judge on a fixed set of stored outputs with known verdicts; if its verdicts change on unchanged outputs, the judge drifted.
M
Walk through the numbers for detecting a 2-point quality drop with 500 judged items a day.

At 85% the daily standard error is √(0.85 × 0.15 / 500) ≈ 1.6 points, so a 3-sigma threshold sits 4.8 points below the mean; a 2-point drop produces a crossing only rarely on any day. In a simulation that took 17 days on average to alarm. An EWMA with λ = 0.2 has a standard deviation one third of the daily one, so its 3-sigma limit is only 1.6 points below the mean, and it alarmed after about 7 days on average, with a comparable false-alarm rate of roughly once in several hundred days. For large drops, say 5 points, both alarm within a day or two.
M
What belongs on the eval dashboard, and what doesn't?

On it: headline quality per product surface with intervals and trend; the comparison between the last release and the current candidate, by slice, with gate status; grader health (judge-human agreement on the latest calibration sample, judge drift check); top failure categories from this week's triage with counts; cost and latency per request; links from every number to example traces. Off it: metrics without an owner or a decision attached, raw counts without intervals, and diagnostics that only matter during an investigation, which belong in drill-down views.
H
Design the CI regression gate for a support assistant, including how you handle flakiness.

Must-pass: 60 cases covering legal, safety and refund-limit behaviour, each run 3 times and required to pass all. Aggregate: policy correctness by a validated judge on 800 cases with 3 samples each, gated by a paired non-inferiority test (candidate − baseline lower 95% bound above −1.5 points). Slices: five pre-declared gate slices with floors and Holm correction. Guardrails: schema validity ≥ 99.5%, p95 latency within 300 ms of baseline, cost per request within 10%. Flakiness: measure A/A noise monthly with ten repeated runs and set the margin above it; replay recorded responses for non-model changes; quarantine and fix flaky cases rather than re-running until green; an override requires a named approver and a written reason.

Follow-up: How do you know the gate catches real regressions? — Seed known-bad variants (a prompt with a policy sentence removed, a cheaper model) and check the gate blocks them; that measures its sensitivity.
H
A provider silently updates the model behind your pinned alias and quality drops 3 points over a week. How should your system have caught it, and how fast?

A scheduled run of the regression suite against production, daily, would show the drop as a paired comparison against the last known-good results, unless the alias changed silently mid-run. The production quality chart with an EWMA would flag a 3-point drop within a few days. A fixed probe set with stored expected outputs and the serving model ID logged on every trace would show a change in the reported model or fingerprint. The fix: pin exact model versions where providers allow, log the model identifier returned by the API, and alert on any change. ae3's GPT-4 drift case is the classic example.
H
How do you close the loop from production failures back to offline evals without overfitting?

Triage sampled and flagged failures weekly, label each with a cause from a failure taxonomy, and turn confirmed failures into eval cases with provenance, generalised into a few variants so the fix addresses the cause rather than the exact wording. Add them to the regression suite or a targeted suite, never to the representative set (ev2). Keep a held-out set and fresh random production samples so you can tell whether the suite still predicts reality. Track the share of production failure categories that are covered by at least one eval case, which measures the suite's coverage of real failures.

Follow-up: The regression suite has grown to 5,000 cases and CI is slow. What then? — Deduplicate near-identical cases, retire cases that haven't failed in months to a nightly tier, and keep the PR tier focused on must-pass and recently failing categories.
H
What would you build first for evaluation infrastructure at a company with three LLM features and no eval tooling?

First, structured tracing with redaction for all three features, because everything else depends on having the data. Second, a minimal shared harness: datasets as versioned files, a runner that calls the system, assertion and judge graders, results stored with their version keys, and a paired comparison report. Third, a small golden set per feature (50-100 real cases) and a CI job running it on prompt or model changes with a simple gate. Fourth, a weekly production sample graded by a judge validated on 100 human labels, and a one-page dashboard. Then iterate: slice floors, control-chart alerts, targeted sampling, red-team suites. Resist building a platform before there are users; the first version should be boring and used.

Follow-up: Buy or build? — Use an existing harness or observability tool where it fits (Inspect, promptfoo, an LLM tracing product) and own the datasets, graders and gates, which are where the product knowledge lives.
